findings.evidence: Synthesis of the findings above. (1): rbuf/ShadowPlay numbers, NvFBC session cost 2.8% at 1,200 fps, and AMD's "lower latency and lower impact" claim. (2): OBS Classic doc and community consensus (no hard data) and the hook design of one GPU copy at Present. (3): OBS PR #2208 timings; rbuf WGC CPU ≈ NvFBC. (4): rbuf OBS display-capture result (1,071 fps, 20.4% dwm.exe CPU). (5): D3DShot ~30% of DDA. Availability: NvFBC is licensed/deprecated, hooks need anti-cheat whitelisting, and CS2 Trusted Mode blocks injection.

design_recommendations: Keep WGC window capture (CreateForWindow on the game HWND) with zero-copy D3D11→NVENC/AMF/QSV as the default. It is the best method that is both legitimately available and anti-cheat-safe for a new app, and it matches where Discord (default on Windows 11), SteelSeries ("Game Capture (WGC)") and Medal (Advanced Window Capture, recommended for CS2) are going. Do not ship any DLL injection or hook: CS2 Trusted Mode blocks it, EAC needs per-game module updates, Vanguard and BattlEye have blocked even OBS and NVIDIA modules.

Do not use NvFBC on Windows. It is deprecated, licensed (GeForce needs NVIDIA's private key), needs admin to enable, and only one process can hold it (it conflicts with NVIDIA Instant Replay). On AMD, consider AMF's proprietary display capture (AMFDisplayCapture) as the monitor-level fallback, since AMD says it beats DDA. On NVIDIA and Intel, use DDA via DuplicateOutput1 for that role.

Fallback chain: (1) WGC window. (2) If the game is in true exclusive fullscreen (no WGC frames, or desktop content where the game should be; Discord uses a Windows API heuristic and falls back), use DDA monitor capture of the game's monitor, or AMF display capture on AMD. Recreate the duplicator on DXGI_ERROR_ACCESS_LOST and run on the adapter that owns the output. (3) WGC monitor capture when DDA can't see the output or on hybrid-GPU laptops (OBS's auto logic). (4) Prompt the user to switch the game to Borderless. Monitor capture also records Discord popups and notifications, so warn the user and crop to the game's rect.

WGC session settings: feature-detect and set MinUpdateInterval (Sunshine uses 4 ms; older builds may cap at 60 fps), call IsBorderRequired(false) after RequestAccessAsync(Borderless) consent (the Windows 11 border setting), use a free-threaded frame pool with 2–3 buffers, and set IsCursorCaptureEnabled(false) (cursor on, since the camera is in-game). Copy each frame into the encoder's input texture immediately so DWM-owned surfaces are not held.

Timestamp every frame with Direct3D11CaptureFrame.SystemRelativeTime (QPC) and every audio packet with the WASAPI QPC position. That gives one local monotonic clock to map onto the peer-synchronized app clock (the global clock the user asked for), with no wall-clock dependency.

Build a PresentMon-based self-test into development and QA. For CS2, Valorant, Fortnite and other popular games in Brazil, measure avg fps, 1% lows and PresentMon presentation mode with capture off, WGC window and DDA. Specifically check whether WGC flips the game from 'Hardware: Independent Flip' to composed mode on systems without MPO, with VRR on and a hardware cursor (Lossless Scaling dev report). Publish the numbers, because no independent benchmark exists.

Use one NVENC session for the ring buffer. Produce the 720p proxy on demand by transcoding the saved range (or a low-cost hardware decode+encode at clip time), not as a second continuous encode, because the GeForce limit of 8 sessions is shared with Discord and ShadowPlay.

Handle capture-blocking and privilege cases: a game using SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE) shows up as an absent window or black frames; non-elevated WGC can't capture elevated windows. Show a clear in-app message rather than silently recording black.

Optional 'perfect sync' mode for demo games (CS2 first, then Dota 2): after the match, fetch the GOTV demo (Valve share code, or Gamers Club/FACEIT demos) and render each friend's POV over the same tick range, either via the Allstar partner API or your own renderer. Market it as a complement, not a replacement: there is no Discord voice (overlay the locally recorded voice track using the synced clock), it is not the literal player screen, there is roughly 30 min render latency, and game updates can break old demos.

Treat the clip-press as an event on the synchronized timeline (like Steam's timeline markers with negative offsets), so both PCs cut N seconds before and M seconds after the same global timestamp. The 1 s keyframe interval already used in the plan (rbuf uses the same default) keeps the clip start within about 1 s of the requested time before trimming.
open_questions: Does WGC window capture measurably change PresentMon presentation mode (independent flip → composed) or add latency in CS2 or Valorant on typical Brazilian hardware (no MPO, G-Sync/FreeSync on)? No controlled study was found.

Do any of the main anti-cheats (Vanguard, EAC, BattlEye, VAC Trusted Mode, FACEIT, Gamers Club AC) block or flag WGC or DDA capture of the game window? No vendor documentation was found, only anecdotes (GGPoker) and Medal/OBS advice that window capture works in CS2 Trusted Mode.
Which Windows build introduced GraphicsCaptureSession.MinUpdateInterval (likely 24H2/26100), and what is WGC's effective frame-rate cap on Windows 10 22H2 and Windows 11 23H2?

What capture path does Xbox Game Bar/bcastdvr use internally? What does AMD ReLive use (presumably the same driver path as AMF display capture)? What exactly does Steam Game Recording use on Windows (presumably the GameOverlayRenderer hook)? None of these is officially documented.
Is Medal's default 'game capture' derived from OBS's graphics-hook, and which anti-cheat whitelists does Medal hold? Not publicly documented.
Is the Allstar partner API open to new third-party apps? Can it render several specific players' POVs over the same tick range, and does Gamers Club expose demos for it?

How reliable is FSE detection in practice (Discord admits false positives)? What share of popular games in Brazil still run in true exclusive fullscreen (Legacy Flip) on Windows 10/11 with fullscreen optimizations?

checks.claim: OBS Game Capture works by injecting graphics-hook64.dll into the game. The 'anti-cheat compatibility hook' is ON by default and loads the DLL through inject-helper with SetWindowsHookEx(WH_GETMESSAGE). When it is off and OBS and the game have the same bitness, OBS injects directly: OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) + VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread(LoadLibraryW). UWP apps never take the anti-cheat path. (R1 and R3)
checks.note: Re-checked at commit c5bcbca. game-capture.c:201-204 `return gc->config.anticheat_hook && !gc->is_app;`. Lines 948-954 choose direct hook vs helper; the log string is "using helper (%s hook)" with "compatibility" or "direct". Line 862 is open_process(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS...). Line 2117 is obs_data_set_default_bool(settings, SETTING_ANTI_CHEAT_HOOK, true). shared/obs-inject-library/inject-library.c:43-54 does virtual_alloc_ex, write_process_memory and create_remote_thread(load_library_w); line 117 is set_windows_hook_ex(WH_GETMESSAGE, proc, lib, thread_id), and the function pointers come from ms_get_obfuscated_func. One detail: when the bitness differs and the anti-cheat hook is off, the helper still does a 'direct' injection. Game Capture is a code-injection method, so it is incompatible with DuoClip's no-injection requirement.

checks.claim: Anti-cheat tolerance of OBS's hook depends on OBS's code-signing certificate. OBS 31.0 (new certificate) broke Game Capture with Vanguard and FACEIT until 31.1. EAC needs per-game module updates, VAC/CS2 Trusted Mode allows no injection, and (R3) Vanguard broke OBS capture again in July 2026. (R1 and R3)
checks.note: Primary, confirmed: the OBS 31.0.0 GitHub release notes say "The code signing certificate for OBS has been updated. This may impact game capture compatibility with some anti-cheat solutions" and point to the KB. compatibility.json has CS2 and CS:GO "may require the -allow_third_party_software launch option to use Game Capture". Unverifiable: the KB's per-vendor table (Vanguard and FACEIT broken on 31.0 and fixed in 31.1, the EAC module footnote, the 2025-06-03 date), the OBS X post, and the July 2026 Vanguard breakage (win.gg). obsproject.com, x.com and win.gg were unreachable, and web search was unavailable. The certificate-change part is confirmed; the vendor-specific details are not.

checks.claim: OBS Game Capture has no WGC or window-capture fallback. When hooking is blocked, compatibility.json tells the user to add Window Capture or Display Capture instead, for example for Destiny 2 and Roblox. (R1)
checks.note: `grep -ci 'wgc\|winrt' plugins/win-capture/game-capture.c` returns 0. compatibility.json:240 reads "Destiny 2 cannot be captured using Game Capture. Use Window Capture or Display Capture instead." Lines 664-676 have a Roblox entry for RobloxPlayerBeta.exe with game_capture:true and the same message, and lines 650-662 say BitBlt cannot capture Roblox. The same file also has 'may require OBS to be run as admin' entries (Call of Duty, Genshin Impact and others). This is OBS's own precedent: for injection-hostile games, non-injection window or display capture is the supported route.

checks.claim: OBS Window Capture 'Automatic' uses BitBlt unless the window class contains 'Chrome' or 'Mozilla', or exactly matches a fixed list (UWP/WinUI, Office, SDL_app, WINDOWSCLIENT (Roblox), WindowsWebview2Wrapper, Gaming Services). WGC is offered only with the D3D11 renderer on build 18362 or later (UniversalApiContract 8). jp9000's 2020 reasons for preferring BitBlt were the border, no cursor control, and the forced switch away from the hardware cursor. (R1 and R3)
checks.note: window-capture.c:113-169 matches the claim exactly, and choose_method returns METHOD_BITBLT by default. plugin-main.c:114 defines win1903 = 18362 and lines 137-138 set wgc_supported only when graphics_uses_d3d11. winrt-capture.cpp:3-7 calls IsApiContractPresent(UniversalApiContract, 8) with the comment 'verify 10.0.18362.0'. Locale strings are 'Legacy (BitBlt)' and 'Modern (WGC)'. The commit 572ce731 message, read on GitHub, matches the quoted reasons, including "switch the cursor away from hardware cursor mode when the capture is active". For DuoClip: OBS does not auto-select WGC for most games; that is OBS's own compatibility choice, not evidence that WGC is worse.

checks.claim: OBS's WGC implementation creates its frame pool with Direct3D11CaptureFramePool::Create (not CreateFreeThreaded) and 2 buffers. Callbacks run through a DispatcherQueue on OBS's graphics thread. Each frame costs one extra CopyResource ('if they gave an SRV, we could avoid this copy'). OBS calls RequestAccessAsync(Borderless) and then IsBorderRequired(false), and sets IsCursorCaptureEnabled when available. (R1 and R3)
checks.note: winrt-capture.cpp:310-313 is Create(device, format, 2, last_size); 316-325 are RequestAccessAsync(GraphicsCaptureAccessKind::Borderless).get(), IsBorderRequired(false) and IsCursorCaptureEnabled(...); 172-173 hold the SRV comment and CopyResource. obs-video.c:1024-1027 runs winrt_dispatcher_init and winrt_capture_thread_start on the graphics thread, and line 1114 has the PeekMessage loop. Extra primary detail from Microsoft's docs (MicrosoftDocs/winrt-api): IsBorderRequired is honored only after the user consents to RequestAccessAsync(Borderless). "If the user denies access, setting this property to false will succeed, but the value will be ignored". The docs also require the graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder capability in the package manifest. OBS is an unpackaged Win32 app and still makes the call; whether an unpackaged app needs that capability is not documented (inferred). CreateFreeThreaded is documented as raising FrameArrived on the pool's internal worker thread, which supports the recommendation to use it on a dedicated thread.

checks.claim: WASAPI process loopback (AUDIOCLIENT_ACTIVATION_TYPE_PROCESS_LOOPBACK + INCLUDE_TARGET_PROCESS_TREE) is documented by Microsoft for build 20348+, but OBS enables it from 19041 ('MS says 20348, but process filtering seems to work earlier'). R2 adds that Medal's 2023 logs show E_UNEXPECTED (0x8000FFFF) activation failures on Windows 10 19045, so a fallback is needed.
checks.note: Confirmed (primary): Microsoft's AUDIOCLIENT_PROCESS_LOOPBACK_PARAMS source doc has req.target-min-winverclnt: Windows 10 Build 20348. OBS win-wasapi/plugin-main.cpp:43-57 has the quoted comment, minimum.build = 19041, and registers the source only then. win-wasapi.cpp:696-709 uses PROCESS_LOOPBACK with INCLUDE_TARGET_PROCESS_TREE and VIRTUAL_AUDIO_DEVICE_PROCESS_LOOPBACK, and line 638 sets a 5 s buffer. Correction to R2's implication: in the public Medal logs (OS 10.0.19045), 'LoopbackCapture::ActivateAudioInterface - failed ... HR 8000FFFF' appears only 4 times (3 in MedalLog20230807, 1 in 20230809). The same logs have many 'Starting GAO...' lines without errors (14+ in 20230803 alone). The failures are intermittent, not systemic, on Windows 10 22H2. Practical reading: enable on 19041+ like OBS, but retry activation, detect failure, and fall back with a warning. Both researchers' recommendations combined are right.

checks.claim: All OBS timing runs on QueryPerformanceCounter. os_gettime_ns() is QPC; encoder packets get system-time DTS (start_ts + relative dts); process-loopback audio uses the WASAPI QPC position × 100. This supports one QPC-based in-app clock with a measured offset between PCs, not each PC's wall clock. (R1)
checks.note: libobs/util/platform-windows.c:391-396: os_gettime_ns calls QueryPerformanceCounter. obs-encoder.c:1408-1411 has the 'we use system time here to ensure sync with other encoders' comment, `pkt->dts_usec = encoder->start_ts / 1000 + packet_dts_usec(pkt) - encoder->offset_usec; pkt->sys_dts_usec = pkt->dts_usec;`, and adds the pause offset. win-wasapi.cpp:1063 is `data.timestamp = ts * 100;` for ProcessOutput. Microsoft's IAudioCaptureClient::GetBuffer doc says pu64QPCPosition = 10,000,000·t/f, 'expressed in 100-nanosecond units', so ×100 gives nanoseconds on the QPC timeline. OBS does not synchronize clocks between machines. The cross-PC offset/drift estimation is DuoClip's own design (inferred), but using QPC rather than wall clock locally is well supported.

checks.claim: WGC frames carry QPC timestamps (Direct3D11CaptureFrame.SystemRelativeTime), the same clock WASAPI uses, so audio and video line up without translation. (R3; R1 recommends using SystemRelativeTime)
checks.note: Confirmed by Microsoft's docs (MicrosoftDocs/winrt-api direct3d11captureframe_systemrelativetime.md): 'The QPC (Query Performance Counter) time at which the compositor rendered the frame.' Sunshine display_wgc.cpp:232 uses it. Caveats: (1) it is the DWM compose time, not the game's Present time or the time the image was on screen. (2) It is a WinRT TimeSpan in 100-ns units; Sunshine's comment 'raw ticks from query performance counter' is loose and is only equal to raw ticks when QPF is 10 MHz (inferred). (3) Sharing a clock domain does not mean zero offset. rbuf measured the click arriving 18 ms after the flash in window capture, and in whole-screen capture the flash appearing 33-44 ms (NvFBC) and 35 ms (WGC) after the click. R3 reported the 35 ms without that direction, which is video lagging audio. DuoClip still needs a per-source A/V offset calibration on top of QPC.

checks.claim: The OBS Replay Buffer is an in-RAM deque of refcounted encoded packets, default 15 s / 500 MB, with the MB cap set to 0 for bitrate-based rate control in Advanced mode. It purges a whole GOP at a time and keeps at least 2 keyframes. Pressing save only records save_ts = QPC now; the save fires when a packet with sys_dts_usec >= save_ts arrives, and muxing goes to obs-ffmpeg-mux.exe. Only 'void save()' and 'get_last_replay' exist, so there is no native post-roll. (R1)
checks.note: obs-ffmpeg-mux.c:917-932 save_replay_proc sets `stream->save_ts = os_gettime_ns() / 1000LL` (and refuses if the encoder is paused). Lines 946-949 register only 'void save()' and 'void get_last_replay(out string path)'. Lines 1031-1046 purge with the `keyframes <= 2` guard for both the size and time caps. Lines 1227-1237 hold the save trigger on sys_dts_usec >= save_ts; if a mux is already running it returns without clearing save_ts, so the save is retried. Lines 1241-1244 set defaults 15 and 500. frontend/utility/AdvancedOutput.cpp:920 is `usesBitrate ? 0 : rbSize`; SimpleOutput.cpp:863 is `usingRecordingPreset ? rbSize : 0`. A grep of obs-ffmpeg-mux.c and frontend for post-roll or delay options found nothing. The R1/R2 post-roll design (save_ts = press + M on the shared clock) is a natural generalization of this mechanism (inferred).

checks.claim: Medal's default 'game capture' injects a hook DLL (medal-hook64.dll) derived from OBS's graphics-hook, and the 2026 recorder still prefers it (PreferGameCapture=true). (R2; R3 says whether Medal is OBS-derived is not publicly documented)
checks.note: Third-party evidence, so secondary. Medal 3.696 logs show '----[ESM State]: OBSInjectionState----', 'Injecting into process', '[OBSCaptureState] Shared texture success' and 'GameRecordingSuccessfullyStarted InjectionCapture' (MedalLog20230803.txt:927-1018). The offsets block at MedalLog20230804.txt:659-671 ([d3d8] present=, [d3d9] present/present_ex/present_swap/d3d9_clsoff/is_d3d9ex_clsoff, [dxgi] present/present1/resize/release) matches the printf sequence in OBS get-graphics-offsets.c:33-45 line for line. The third-party extraction of recorder v2638.2751.1 (recorder_metadata.json) contains MedalEncoder.OBS.HookInterface, BaseHookInterface and GraphicsOffsets, and FINDINGS.md:49 describes Host injection helpers and Licenses/obs_source_offer.txt. settings_catalog.json defaults: PreferGameCapture=True, ForceWindowCapture=False, AdvancedWindowCapture=False. Not verified first-hand: the Frida 'medal_temp_d3d_window_4039785' trace, and Medal's own support text (support.medal.tv unreachable). R2's position is better supported than R3's 'not documented'.

checks.claim: Medal's 'Advanced Window Capture' is Windows.Graphics.Capture, and its standard non-injected window capture (2023) was DXGI-based, probably Desktop Duplication cropped to the window, which explains the 'Game out of Focus' placeholder. (R2; R3 infers AWC=WGC from the yellow border)
checks.note: AWC = WGC is supported by the logs: MedalLog20230809.txt:283 'Executing Request: set.windowsGraphicsCapture' and :287 'Saving Advanced Window Capture 0'; the settings JSON key is set.windowsGraphicsCapture. Standard mode, confirmed in the logs: for Roblox (Win32), 'Capture area is 0,24,1920,1040' (:492), 'Creating overlay frame from ...\Assets\inactiveGame.png' (:507), 'WindowCaptureStandard' (:512), and 'Capture mode: DXGI' in other sessions (MedalLog20230803.txt:534). That this is Desktop Duplication cropped to the window is an inference, not confirmed. Medal's claims that AWC works when minimized and fails in exclusive fullscreen are unverifiable here (support.medal.tv unreachable).

checks.claim: Medal supports post-roll for event-triggered clips by delaying the replay-buffer snapshot (Game API captureDelayMs: 'Milliseconds Medal waits after the request before snapshotting the replay buffer'). The manual hotkey only looks backward. (R2)
checks.note: The captureDelayMs wording is confirmed in YoYoGames/GMEXT-Medal spec/medal-openapi.yaml:103-108: "Milliseconds Medal waits after the request before snapshotting the replay buffer. Useful for catching a killcam or another post-action moment." That is a third-party transcription (secondary). Medal's own developer pages (medal.tv/developer/...) and the support article saying the hotkey saves only preceding footage could not be fetched (medal.tv blocked). The mechanism (delay the snapshot by M seconds) matches the OBS save_ts mechanism and is the right model for DuoClip's post-roll.

checks.claim: Medal's 2026 marketing pages claim 'Medal does not inject into games or interact with anti-cheat systems', while its support docs say 'Medal injects into your games so that it can give you an overlay and capture your gameplay'. (R2)
checks.note: medal.tv and support.medal.tv were unreachable (ENOTFOUND/403), and web search was unavailable, so neither quote could be checked first-hand. Indirectly, the shipped recorder evidence (OBSInjectionState logs; MedalEncoder.OBS.* classes in 2026 metadata; default PreferGameCapture=True) contradicts a blanket 'does not inject' claim, but it does not show what the 2026 recorder does in each anti-cheat-protected title.

checks.claim: NVIDIA deprecated NvFBC on Windows 10+ (frozen at Capture SDK 7.1, last supported build 1803) and it is not legitimately available to third parties on GeForce. Workarounds pass NVIDIA's private key, need admin to enable, and only one client can hold it; ShadowPlay uses NvFBC. (R3)
checks.note: Confirmed (secondary): the rbuf README says GeForce 'only grants NvFBC sessions to callers that pass a private-data key' and that rbuf passes NVIDIA's own (lines 101-103). It also documents `--nvfbc-enable` (as administrator) and nvsphelper64.exe holding NvFBC while Instant Replay runs. keylase/nvidia-patch nvfbcwrp README: 'Wrapper for NvFBC64.dll library which injects private keys into NvFBC_CreateEx calls', made by replacing system32 DLLs. AlwaysShadow issue #20 quotes ShadowPlay's CaptureCore.log 'NvFBCH264GrabFrame failed with error = NVFBC_ERROR_PROTECTED_CONTENT'. Sunshine docs mark nvfbc 'Applies to Linux only'. Unverifiable: NVIDIA's bulletin text ('frozen at 7.1', 'last supported 1803'), because developer.nvidia.com and developer.download.nvidia.com were blocked. Nuance: 'deprecated' does not mean non-functional. rbuf runs NvFBC on Windows 11 23H2 with driver 610.88. Excluding it for DuoClip is still correct on licensing grounds (private key) and the admin-only switch.

checks.claim: The only hard numbers (rbuf, single machine): at 1,218 fps the game ran at 1,164 fps with NvFBC, 1,158 with ShadowPlay and 1,071 with OBS display capture (9.9% CPU plus 20.4% in dwm.exe), and WGC CPU cost was about equal to NvFBC (1.93% vs 1.87%). R3 uses this to rank 'WGC monitor / DDA' as heavier than 'WGC window'.
checks.note: The numbers match the rbuf README (lines 9-18 and the 125-130 table). Caveats R3 dropped: (1) the 1.93% vs 1.87% figures are rbuf's own process CPU in a separate test (ffplay test pattern, 60 s buffer), comparing WGC+H.264 with NvFBC+H.264. They are not a game-FPS impact measurement, and WGC was never benchmarked on game FPS there. (2) The rbuf table does not say which API 'OBS Studio (display capture)' used (DXGI vs WGC), and the figure includes OBS's whole compositor/scaling pipeline, so it cannot be attributed to DDA. (3) rbuf is a v0.4.0 single-author project with no binary release. R3's ranking that places DDA below WGC window is therefore inference, not measurement. R1 and R3 agree that no controlled benchmark exists. Separately, OBS PR #2208 (merged 2020-02-23) reported WGC 'a bit more expensive than BitBlt ... maybe 200-800 us vs 300-500 us' and 'a bit cheaper than BitBlt on GPU', confirmed by reading the PR.

checks.claim: WGC may be capped at 60 fps unless GraphicsCaptureSession.MinUpdateInterval is set (newer builds, likely 24H2/26100). (R3)
checks.note: Sunshine display_wgc.cpp:159-165 sets MinUpdateInterval(4ms) // 250Hz when IsPropertyPresent. It logs 'Can't set MinUpdateInterval on this version of Windows' if absent, and the '...may be capped to 60fps...' text only when setting it throws. The 60 fps cap is Sunshine's warning text, not Microsoft documentation. The MicrosoftDocs/winrt-api repo has no MinUpdateInterval page for GraphicsCaptureSession (only LampArray's), so the build is unconfirmed from primary sources. Win32CaptureSample issue #82 is a user report with no Microsoft reply. It refers to 'the new 26100 APIs' and reports that the default 0 (or <1 ms) capped capture at about 50 fps on 144 fps content, while values >=1 ms behaved as expected. DuoClip should feature-detect it, set it explicitly, and measure the delivered fps.

checks.claim: Discord's default capture injects a signed DLL (overlay technology). WGC is available on Windows 10+, Discord says it will make WGC the default on Windows 11, and WGC does not work for full-screen exclusive games. (R3)
checks.note: support.discord.com was unreachable from this environment (ENOTFOUND/403), and web search was unavailable, so the quoted article could not be checked. The FSE limitation is consistent with rbuf's test (in exclusive fullscreen, 'Windows Graphics Capture's [frame] is the desktop', with PresentMon showing Legacy Flip). Microsoft documents that Desktop Duplication becomes invalid (DXGI_ERROR_ACCESS_LOST) on a 'Switch from DWM on, DWM off, or other full-screen application' and must be recreated. That supports a DDA fallback with re-creation logic.

checks.claim: The GeForce NVENC concurrent-session limit is 8 per system (Video Codec SDK 12.2 note, driver >= 551.76), shared with everything else encoding on the PC. (R3)
checks.note: NVIDIA's support matrix and forums (developer.nvidia.com, forums.developer.nvidia.com) were blocked, and web search was unavailable. The keylase/nvidia-patch README only says NVIDIA imposes a session limit on consumer GPUs, without a number. The design advice (one continuous encode, proxy made on demand) is sound whatever the exact limit.

contradictions_between_researchers: Where Medal's hook comes from: R2 says Medal's default game hook is derived from OBS graphics-hook and ships an OBS source offer. R3 says this is 'not publicly documented', and its claim and open question say it was not found. My check supports R2. Medal's 2023 log prints the OBS get-graphics-offsets format line for line, and the 2026 recorder metadata has MedalEncoder.OBS.HookInterface/GraphicsOffsets. This is still third-party (secondary) evidence.

Process loopback on Windows 10: R1 recommends enabling it on build 19041+ as OBS does. R2 stresses Microsoft's 20348 minimum and Medal's 0x8000FFFF failures on 19045, and recommends an endpoint-loopback fallback. The public Medal 19045 logs show only intermittent failures (4 occurrences) among many successful GAO starts. Both are partly right: enable on 19041+, detect failure and fall back.

Efficiency ranking: R1 reports no official benchmark, and OBS forum replies treat the methods as a compatibility choice. R3 publishes a ranking (driver < hook < WGC window < WGC monitor/DDA < BitBlt) based mainly on one rbuf 'OBS display capture' number. That number does not identify DXGI vs WGC and includes OBS's compositor, so the ranking below 'hook' is inference.

Cursor setting: R3 recommends 'IsCursorCaptureEnabled(false) (cursor on, since the camera is in-game)', which contradicts itself, because false means the cursor is not captured. R1 says to set it as wanted. OBS sets it from capture_cursor && cursor_visible.

A/V timing: R3 says WGC and WASAPI QPC timestamps 'line up without translation'. R1 notes that OBS timestamps video on its render grid rather than at capture. Microsoft defines SystemRelativeTime as the compositor render time, and rbuf measured 18-44 ms A/V offsets, so a per-source calibration offset is still needed even though the clock domain is shared.

Medal's statements: R2 cites 2026 Medal marketing saying 'does not inject into games', while R2 and R3 both cite Medal support saying it uses a hook or injects. This is an internal Medal inconsistency, and neither page could be fetched here.

Medal standard window capture: R2 infers DXGI Desktop Duplication cropped to the window (log: 'Capture mode: DXGI', capture-area rect). R3 only says Medal mentions DXGI capture without naming the API. These are compatible, but R2's crop interpretation is unconfirmed.
verification.corrections_summary:
I re-checked 18 decision-relevant claims. The OBS source claims all hold at commit c5bcbca: Game Capture is DLL injection, with the SetWindowsHookEx compatibility hook on by default; Game Capture has no WGC fallback; Window Capture's Automatic mode prefers BitBlt; the WGC path uses 2 buffers, an extra CopyResource and a Borderless request; process loopback is enabled on 19041+ although Microsoft documents 20348; all timing is QPC; the replay buffer is a RAM deque purged per GOP, saves on save_ts, and has no native post-roll. Microsoft's docs also confirm that WGC SystemRelativeTime is QPC-based and that WASAPI QPCPosition is in 100-ns units.

Corrections:
1. Medal's process-loopback failures on Windows 10 19045 are intermittent (4 occurrences among many successes), not systemic. Enable it on 19041+ and fall back on failure.
2. SystemRelativeTime is the DWM compose time, not the game's Present time. Measured A/V offsets of 18-44 ms mean a calibration offset is still needed on top of the shared QPC clock.
3. rbuf's 'WGC ≈ NvFBC CPU' figure is rbuf's own process CPU in a separate test, not a game-FPS measurement. Its 'OBS display capture' run does not say whether it used DXGI or WGC. R3's ranking below 'hook' is therefore inference.
4. The WGC 60 fps cap is Sunshine's warning text, not Microsoft documentation. MinUpdateInterval has no Microsoft doc page. A user report (Win32CaptureSample #82, build 26100) says the default of 0 gave about 50 fps.
5. IsBorderRequired(false) is silently ignored unless the user consents to RequestAccessAsync(Borderless). The docs also require a graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder package capability; how this applies to unpackaged apps is undocumented.
6. NvFBC is deprecated but still functional on Windows 11 with NVIDIA's private key and an admin-only enable. Excluding it remains correct for licensing reasons. NVIDIA's own bulletin wording could not be verified.
7. Third-party evidence supports Medal's OBS-derived injected hook, its default PreferGameCapture=true, Advanced Window Capture being WGC, and captureDelayMs post-roll.
8. R3's cursor recommendation contradicts itself.

These are unverifiable because the egress proxy blocked the hosts and the session's web search budget was used up: OBS KB vendor table details, Discord's default-capture article, the SteelSeries 'Game Capture (WGC)' label, Steam recording internals, the NVENC 8-session limit, and Medal's own support and marketing wording. Blocked hosts included learn.microsoft.com, obsproject.com, support.discord.com, medal.tv, nvidia.com and steampowered.com, so Microsoft docs were read from the MicrosoftDocs GitHub source repos instead. Downloads are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-code/d9f782f3-49d0-5a92-afb7-40a0c0d80994/scratchpad/dl-fc-obs, dl-fc-msdocs, dl-fc-medal, dl-fc-nv and dl-fc-ow (read and grep only).

research.topic: Design input: in-app GLOBAL CLOCK (QPC disciplined to UTC via authenticated NTP/NTS, plus P2P refinement) for timestamping every DuoClip clip across 2–5 Windows PCs in Brazil
research.summary:
The user is right not to trust the Windows clock. Microsoft says the default W32Time setup only aims at Kerberos-level, "loosely accurate" time. A standalone PC syncs to time.windows.com with SpecialPollInterval = 604,800 s, and since build 1703 that value is capped by MaxPollInterval = 2^15 s. In practice that means one sync every ~9 h or less often (the ~9 h figure is my inference). W32Time slews offsets up to MaxAllowedPhaseOffset, which is 1 s on standalone machines, and steps the clock for anything larger. Secure Time Seeding can set grossly wrong dates, and users can change the clock by hand. Microsoft's own support boundary requires <5 ms latency, ≤6 hops and stratum ≤5 even for the 50 ms tier, and says "for 1 ms accuracy, you can't depend on remote time sources". Home PCs on the Internet don't meet the 50 ms tier conditions.

QPC is a better base. It is monotonic, unaffected by system-time changes, leap seconds and DST, has <1 µs resolution, and keeps counting through sleep. It is also the native timebase of both capture paths: WGC Direct3D11CaptureFrame.SystemRelativeTime and WASAPI pu64QPCPosition (100 ns units). So the "global clock" should be an app-internal mapping UTC_ns = f(QPC) with a continuously estimated offset and frequency. The app's own NTS client feeds it, and the app never touches the OS clock, so it needs no admin rights and stays anti-cheat friendly.

Best public sources for Brazil: NTP.br stratum-1 servers (a/b/c/d.st1.ntp.br, plus gps.ntp.br on GPS) are fed by Observatório Nacional cesium clocks, and NIC.br says NTS is enabled on its stratum-1 servers. time.cloudflare.com is anycast, has NTS (NTS-KE on port 4460, TLS 1.3), does not smear, and Cloudflare reports 25+ Brazilian cities. Avoid Google and AWS (both leap-smear, and mixing smeared with non-smeared sources is explicitly discouraged). Avoid time.windows.com (no NTS found, and SIDN observed Microsoft servers up to 50 ms off for hours). Avoid hard-coding pool.ntp.org (no NTS, and the vendor-zone policy forbids it). IETF Roughtime has only 1-second resolution, so it is useful only as a coarse sanity check.

The error bound for any NTP-style exchange is RTT/2 (path asymmetry); NTS cannot fix this because it doesn't stop delay attacks. Two clients synced to a common UTC source have a relative error ≤ δA/2 + δB/2. A direct P2P measurement has an error ≤ δAB/2. The global approach wins when friends are in different cities but each is near a server (for example Cloudflare's or NTP.br's local presence). P2P wins or ties when friends share a city or ISP, and it is the only option when UDP 123 is blocked. A hybrid is the most robust: UTC as the canonical clip timescale, plus P2P NTP-style pings over an unordered, unreliable WebRTC data channel during a session as a cross-check and refinement. Expected relative error with min-RTT filtering is roughly 1–5 ms on wired fiber, a few ms more on Wi-Fi, and 5–50 ms on 4G. These expectations are inferred; I found no Brazil-specific measurements, so the app should collect telemetry.

For sub-frame sync, store raw QPC plus the mapping, and re-map clips after the fact using sync samples from both before and after the clip. Carry the hotkey press as a global timestamp so that message delivery delay doesn't matter. Keep the live clock slew-only (monotonic). Persist the frequency estimate like chrony's driftfile. Store start_utc_ns plus an explicit uncertainty in every clip.

Perfect clocks still won't make the two POVs show events at exactly the same instant, because game netcode interpolates (Source engine default is 100 ms). The editor should show the uncertainty and offer a manual or audio-assisted nudge.

For Rust: ntp-proto 1.9.0 (Apache-2.0 OR MIT) has NTS-KE, packet code and a Kalman filter, but says it gives no API stability guarantee. rkik-nts 1.4.0 (MIT) is a high-level NTS client but takes t1/t4 from SystemTime, so it needs a small fork to use QPC. sntpc (MIT OR Apache-2.0) allows a custom timestamp source but has no NTS. rsntp (MIT OR Apache-2.0) is SNTP-only and measures against the system clock.

findings.claim: The Windows default time configuration is designed for Kerberos and 'loosely accurate' time, not high accuracy.
findings.evidence: configuring-systems-for-high-accuracy.md lines 22-29: 'the default configuration is intended to satisfy the same requirements as prior operating systems that: Provide the necessary time accuracy to satisfy Kerberos version 5 authentication requirements. Provide loosely accurate time...'. accurate-time.md line 57: Kerberos 'requires 5 minutes of accuracy'.

findings.claim: Standalone (non-domain) Windows polls time.windows.com very rarely by default: SpecialPollInterval is 604,800 s (1 week), and since build 1703 it is clamped by MinPollInterval=10 (1024 s) and MaxPollInterval=15 (32768 s ≈ 9.1 h). The effective interval is therefore about 9 h at best (my inference). Users report syncs being missed even after tweaking these values.
findings.evidence: Windows-Time-Service-Tools-and-Settings.md line 377: 'SpecialPollInterval ... The default value on stand-alone clients and servers is 604,800. Starting with build 1703, SpecialPollInterval is contained by the MinPollInterval and MaxPollInterval'. Lines 341/344: MaxPollInterval standalone 15, MinPollInterval standalone 10. Line 296: NtpServer default 'time.windows.com, 0x9'. Forum and Microsoft Q&A reports of unreliable sync intervals appear in the elevenforum and pretentiousname pages.

findings.claim: W32Time slews small offsets and steps large ones. On standalone PCs the step threshold is only 1 s, phase correction is slow (PhaseCorrectRate 7, UpdateInterval 360,000 × 10 ms), and corrections above 15 h are only logged, not applied. The OS clock can therefore jump, and it can also stay wrong for long periods.
findings.evidence: Tools-and-Settings.md lines 103-106: 'CurrentTimeOffset ≤ MaxAllowedPhaseOffset: Adjust the computer clock gradually by using the clock rate. CurrentTimeOffset > MaxAllowedPhaseOffset: Set the computer clock immediately.' Line 338: MaxAllowedPhaseOffset 'default value for stand-alone clients and servers is 1' (domain 300). Lines 340/342: Max{Neg,Pos}PhaseCorrection standalone 54,000 s (15 h); larger corrections are logged instead. Line 345: PhaseCorrectRate standalone 7. Line 349: UpdateInterval standalone 360,000. Improvements doc: 'Windows doesn't step time, unless certain bounds are exceeded, but instead disciplines the clock.'

findings.claim: Microsoft's high-accuracy support boundary: 1 s, 50 ms and 1 ms tiers each need a special configuration (registry changes need admin) and tight network conditions that home Internet users generally can't meet below the 1 s tier.
findings.evidence: 1 s tier: Windows 10+, an NTP hierarchy ending at an accurate source, all Windows nodes configured per 'Configuring Systems for High Accuracy', cumulative one-way latency ≤100 ms. 50 ms tier adds: '<5 ms of network latency between its time source', stratum ≤5, 'six or fewer network hops', daily CPU ≤90%. 1 ms tier adds: '<0.1 ms latency', 'four or fewer network hops', CPU ≤80%. accurate-time.md line 35: 'For 1 ms accuracy, you can't depend on a remote time sources.' The high-accuracy config sets Min/MaxPollInterval=6 (64 s) and UpdateInterval=100.

findings.claim: Microsoft itself warns that time.windows.com may not be a stable or local source, and that asymmetric paths and network load reduce accuracy.
findings.evidence: windows-server-2016-improvements.md line 144: 'Using the default of time.windows.com might not provide a stable and local time source.' accurate-time.md line 35: standalone machines use time.windows.com; 'Network traffic loads and asymmetrical network paths may reduce the accuracy'. The 'Symmetrical NTP communication' section says the calculations 'assume the network path is symmetrical'.

findings.claim: Secure Time Seeding (UtilizeSslTimeData) is on by default in client Windows. It has been reported to set wildly wrong dates, for example decades or more ahead, which is one more way the OS clock can jump.
findings.evidence: Tools-and-Settings.md line 350: UtilizeSslTimeData default '1 except for Windows Server 2025, where the default value is 0'. The high-accuracy guide disables it (value 0). Kaspersky, citing Ars Technica (2023), describes STS resetting the time; ctrl.blog reports Windows thinking 40,689 days had passed.

findings.claim: Microsoft time servers have been measured out of sync by up to 50 ms for hours. In a seven-provider study, Cloudflare was the only provider supporting NTS. Anycast providers could only be partly evaluated, one site per vantage point.
findings.evidence: SIDN Labs BigTime report (Dec 2025 / Jun 2026), as quoted in search results: 'three of Microsoft's servers were out-of-sync during our measurements, by up to 50ms'. Cloudflare was the only one with NTS, RPKI, DNSSEC and IPv6 together. 'our VPs can reach only a single site (location) of anycast providers (Google, Cloudflare, and Meta)'. The PDF itself was blocked by the research proxy.

findings.claim: I found no evidence that W32Time or time.windows.com support NTS. The default Windows source is unauthenticated for standalone PCs.
findings.evidence: Searches returned only legacy domain Kerberos-signed NTP docs (Windows Server 2008 era) and nothing on NTS for Windows 11, Server 2025 or time.windows.com.

findings.claim: QPC is the right local base for an app clock. It is monotonic, unaffected by system-time changes, leap seconds or time zones, has sub-µs resolution, counts through sleep, and is not synchronized to UTC. GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime returns UTC with <1 µs precision, but its accuracy is whatever W32Time achieves.
findings.evidence: acquiring-high-resolution-time-stamps.md line 13: 'QPC is independent of, and isn't synchronized to, any external time reference'. Line 189: 'QPC is completely independent of the system time and UTC' (re DST, leap seconds, admin changes). Line 270+: 'Is the performance counter monotonic? Yes. QPC does not go backward.' Line 380: QPC counts ticks 'including the time when the machine was in a sleep state'. GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime: 'highest possible level of precision (<1us)'. The improvements doc says it returns 'System Time, which is conditioned by the Windows Time service'.

findings.claim: A free-running PC oscillator drifts quickly: ±10 ppm is ±36 ms per hour (±0.86 s/day), and 100 ppm is 8.64 s/day. QPC must therefore be frequency-disciplined, not just offset-corrected. Oscillator stability depends on temperature changes, which matters on a gaming PC under load.
findings.evidence: QPC doc table: '1 hour ± 36 milliseconds; 1 day ± 0.86 seconds' at ±10 ppm, and 'a frequency error of 100 ppm causes an error of 8.64 seconds after 24 hours'. chrony FAQ: clock stability 'mainly depends on the temperature sensitivity of the crystal oscillator and the maximum rate of the temperature change'.

findings.claim: Both capture paths already timestamp in the QPC domain, so the app clock can map media timestamps to global time directly without reading the system clock.
findings.evidence: WinRT docs: Direct3D11CaptureFrame.SystemRelativeTime is 'The QPC (Query Performance Counter) time at which the compositor rendered the frame.' WASAPI IAudioCaptureClient::GetBuffer: pu64QPCPosition is 'the value of the performance counter at the time that the audio endpoint device recorded the device position of the first audio frame', computed as 10,000,000·t/f (100-ns units).

findings.claim: In Rust on Windows, std::time::Instant is QPC and SystemTime::now() is GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime. Any crate that uses SystemTime for t1/t4 measures against the OS clock.
findings.evidence: rust-lang/rust library/std/src/sys/pal/windows/time.rs line 29: perf_counter::now() calls c::QueryPerformanceCounter. library/std/src/sys/time/windows.rs line 77: c::GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime (c.rs line 416 falls back to GetSystemTimeAsFileTime for legacy targets).

findings.claim: NTP.br (NIC.br) runs public stratum-1 servers a.st1, b.st1, c.st1 and d.st1.ntp.br, fed by Observatório Nacional cesium clocks, plus gps.ntp.br (GPS). NIC.br states NTS is available on its stratum-1 servers and recommends using it. NTS on its stratum-2 servers was still being completed.
findings.evidence: ntp.br/conteudo/estrutura (via search): primary stratum-1 servers 'sincronizados com relógios atômicos' of ON; gps.ntp.br stratum 1 GPS. ntp.br homepage (via search snippet): 'O NTP.br já disponibiliza o NTS em seus servidores stratum 1 e é recomendável que todos o utilizem'. A NIC.br presentation says NTS has been operational on stratum 1 since 2021, with stratum 2 in progress. The jauderho/nts-servers list includes a/b/c.st1 and gps (stratum 1) and d.st1 (listed as stratum 2). IPs: a.st1 200.160.7.186 / 2001:12ff:0:7::186. ntp.br was unreachable from the research environment, so this is based on search snippets.

findings.claim: NTP.br is expanding regionally: a 2026 ETICE/NIC.br station in Fortaleza (cesium and GNSS, e.g. gps.ce.ntp.br) is claimed to give Northeast users latency under 1 ms. Cesium clocks are in São Paulo, Rio and Brasília.
findings.evidence: ETICE dossier and IX Fórum Fortaleza (24 Mar 2026) coverage, via search: Fortaleza station, 'gps.ce.ntp.br (Sincronizado diretamente ao sistema de satélites GNSS)'. The latency claim is the institution's own and has not been independently measured.

findings.claim: time.cloudflare.com is a free anycast NTP/NTS service that does not leap-smear and warns against mixing smeared and non-smeared servers. Its NTS-KE moved to the IANA port 4460 when RFC 8915 was published. Cloudflare reports 25+ Brazilian cities, but I found no public accuracy measurements for its Brazilian PoPs.
findings.evidence: cloudflare-docs time-services/ntp/index.mdx: 'Cloudflare does not implement leap smearing ... Using servers that smear time along with servers that do not may lead to unpredictable and anomalous results.' nts.mdx: NTS per RFC 8915, NTS-KE via TLS, then NTS extension fields; point clients at time.cloudflare.com. ntp/usage.mdx: IPs 162.159.200.1, 162.159.200.123, 2606:4700:f1::1, 2606:4700:f1::123. The 'NTS is now an RFC' blog (2020) reports the move to port 4460. The 'Expanding to 25+ cities in Brazil' blog reports 25th-percentile latency dropping to sub-10 ms for web traffic, not NTP. jauderho's list gives time.cloudflare.com as stratum 3, anycast.

findings.claim: Google Public NTP and AWS time.aws.com both leap-smear (24 h linear, noon to noon UTC), and both vendors say not to mix smeared and non-smeared servers. Mixing them with NTP.br or Cloudflare would cause up to 0.5 s disagreement around a leap second. I found no NTS support for Google.
findings.evidence: Google smear page and FAQ (via search): 'We recommend that you don't configure Google Public NTP together with non-leap-smearing NTP servers'; the FAQ lists only NTP/SNTP v3/v4. AWS: 'smooths the addition or removal of the leap second with a 24-hour linear smear from noon to noon UTC', 'AWS does not recommend using both smeared and non-smeared time sources'. developers.google.com was unreachable, so Google is based on search snippets.

findings.claim: The NTP Pool Brazil zone has roughly 24–25 active IPv4 servers, offers no NTS (an NTS pool exists only as an experiment, with an IETF draft), and its vendor policy forbids shipping the standard pool names as an application's default without a vendor zone.
findings.evidence: ntppool.org/zone/br: 'There are 24/25 active servers in this zone' (IPv4). Trifecta Tech runs an experimental NTS pool (experimental.ntspooltest.org); draft-ietf-ntp-nts-keyexchange-pool-00 (Mar 2026) is Experimental. ntppool.org/vendors bars using the standard zone names as the default configuration of an application.

findings.claim: NTS (RFC 8915) authenticates the server through TLS 1.3 NTS-KE (TCP 4460), then protects NTP packets over UDP 123 with AEAD extension fields and one-time cookies (8 by default). This blocks spoofing, modification and replay. Time values themselves are not secret.
findings.evidence: ntpd-rs ntp-proto/src/nts/mod.rs line 27: 'const DEFAULT_NUMBER_OF_COOKIES: usize = 8'. Line 338: client_config_builder_with_protocol_versions(&[&TLS13]). docs/man/ntp.toml.5.md line 100: NTS-KE 'default port is 4460'. docs/guide/nts.md: goals are server identity verification, packet authenticity and replay prevention; 'the time information itself is considered public information and as such is not encrypted'. Cloudflare nts.mdx describes the two phases.

findings.claim: NTS cannot stop delay attacks or natural path asymmetry. An on-path attacker or an asymmetric route can bias the offset by up to about RTT/2. Mitigations are an RTT cap and multiple independent servers and paths.
findings.evidence: Weberblog: delayed packets 'are still valid and difficult to detect ... results in a systematic time offset'; 'maximum possible time offset ... about half of the RTT. If the maximum permitted runtime is set to 300 milliseconds, the possible time offset ... ±150 milliseconds'. arXiv 2407.13386: content is authenticated, but 'the adversary can manipulate the measured arrival times via man-in-the-middle delays'. RFC 8915 has a 'Delay Attacks' subsection (text not retrieved).

findings.claim: NTS-KE depends on TLS certificate validity checks, so a PC whose clock is far off (for example after an STS mis-seed) can fail NTS bootstrap. chrony works around this with 'nocerttimecheck' as a last resort.
findings.evidence: chrony.conf.adoc line 998: 'nocerttimecheck ... disables the checks of the activation and expiration times of certificates for the specified number of clock updates. It allows the NTS authentication mechanism to be used on computers which start with the wrong time ... should be used only as a last resort'.

findings.claim: IETF Roughtime (draft-ietf-ntp-roughtime-19, Experimental, in the RFC Editor queue as of March 2026) uses whole-second timestamps and a radius in seconds, so it is useless for ms-level sync. It is only a cheap signed sanity check against gross clock errors. Cloudflare runs a beta server.
findings.evidence: Draft source: 'A timestamp is a representation of UTC time as a uint64 count of seconds since ... Unix epoch'; 'The RADI tag value is a uint32 representing the server's estimate of the accuracy of MIDP in seconds ... MUST NOT be zero ... Servers that do not have any leap second information SHOULD set ... RADI to at least 3'. Cloudflare: roughtime.cloudflare.com:2003, public key 0GD7c3yP8xEc4Zl2zeuN2SlLvDVVocjsPSL8/Rl/7zg= (beta, key may change); positioned for 'within 10 seconds' use cases.

findings.claim: No leap second will occur at the end of December 2026 (IERS Bulletin C 72, 6 July 2026). UTC−TAI stays at −37 s, and leap seconds are slated for abolition by 2035. Leap-second handling is low-risk but should still be designed in.
findings.evidence: Bulletin C 72 (forwarded to the tz list): 'NO leap second will be introduced at the end of December 2026', UTC-TAI = -37 s. The CGPM 2022 decision to abolish leap seconds by 2035 is cited in the coverage.

findings.claim: Typical Internet NTP accuracy is a few milliseconds and is limited by path asymmetry. The maximum asymmetry error is half the round-trip delay. Wireless links with long delays are often highly asymmetric.
findings.evidence: chrony README: 'Typical accuracy between two machines synchronised over the Internet is within a few milliseconds'. chrony FAQ: 'Half of the root delay is the maximum error due to asymmetric delays'; 'estimated maximum error ... is the sum of the root dispersion and half of the root delay (root distance)'. chrony.conf maxdelay: 'particularly so on wireless networks and other slow links, where a long delay probably indicates a highly asymmetric delay'. NIST (Novick & Lombardi): WAN asymmetry 'typically limits NTP time transfer uncertainty to about one millisecond'.

findings.claim: Over 4G/LTE, naive NTP often shows errors above 50 ms. Expert estimates for SNTP over LTE are around 100 ms and depend on the operator. I found no Brazil-specific residential, fiber or 4G NTP accuracy measurements.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2306.00633: wired LAN about 1 ms; 'a clock synchronization error of more than 50 ms was frequently observed when we directly applied NTP in the wireless network'. Nordic DevZone: 'Maybe around 100 ms could be achievable, but highly dependent on the network operator'. No Brazilian measurement was found.

findings.claim: Error bounds for the architectures, from the standard NTP offset/delay math. (i) Both clients synced to UTC servers: |eA−eB| ≤ δA/2 + δB/2 + εSA + εSB, where δ is the client–server RTT and ε the server's own error. Errors partly cancel when both use the same server over similar ISP paths. (ii) Direct P2P: |eAB| ≤ δAB/2, where δAB is the peer RTT (larger if relayed through TURN). Example: an SP user and a Recife user each near a server (δ≈5–10 ms) give a bound of about 5–10 ms globally, versus δAB≈50 ms giving 25 ms for P2P. Two users in the same city (δAB≈10 ms) give about 5 ms with either.
findings.evidence: Derived from θ=((t2−t1)+(t3−t4))/2, δ=(t4−t1)−(t3−t2) and the chrony FAQ half-RTT bound. The RTT numbers are illustrative and not measured.

findings.claim: Classic NTP keeps the sample with the lowest delay from the last 8, because offset error grows with delay. The true offset lies within θ0 ± (δ−δ0)/2. chrony instead uses weighted linear regression with delay-based rejection (maxdelay, maxdelayratio, maxdelaydevratio 10, maxdelayquant).
findings.evidence: Mills clock filter: 'δ0 is estimated as the minimum of the last eight delay measurements'; 'The correct time θ must lie within the wedge θ0 ± (δ − δ0)/2'. chrony.conf: maxdelay default 3 s; maxdelaydevratio default 10.0; 'maxdelayquant 0.2 would indicate that only measurements with the lowest 20 percent of round-trip delays should be accepted'; polltarget is the 'Target number of measurements to use for the regression algorithm'.

findings.claim: chrony defaults are a good template for polling and slewing. For Internet servers: minpoll 6 (64 s), maxpoll 10 (1024 s), polltarget 8. Default max slew rate is 83,333 ppm. Leap modes include slew and ignore. Mixing authenticated and unauthenticated sources should be avoided.
findings.evidence: chrony FAQ: 'default values are 6 (64 seconds) for minpoll, 10 (1024 seconds) for maxpoll and 8 (samples) for polltarget. The default values should be used for general servers on the Internet'; 'Mixing of authenticated and unauthenticated servers should generally be avoided'. chrony.conf maxslewrate: 'By default, the maximum slew rate is set to 83333.333 ppm'; leapsecmode system/step/slew/ignore.

findings.claim: ntpd-rs uses a Kalman-filter clock algorithm (offset and frequency with uncertainties). In ntp-proto 1.9.0 it is ntp_proto::algorithm::kalman. On main it has moved to an unpublished 'statime-algo' crate with an UncertainValue type and time_to_error_bound_exceedance(). Tweede Golf estimates measurement noise from RTT variation and models process noise as a frequency random walk.
findings.evidence: raw ntpd-rs v1.9.0 ntp-proto/src/algorithm/kalman/mod.rs exists (HTTP 200); lib.rs line 146 'mod algorithm'. main: statime-algo/src/estimator.rs has 'pub struct UncertainValue', 'clock_offset', 'clock_frequency', 'time_to_error_bound_exceedance'. crates.io: 'crate statime-algo does not exist'. Tweede Golf slides: 'measurement noise is estimated through variation of round trip delay; process noise assumes a frequency random walk'.

findings.claim: Rust NTP/NTS crates and licenses (crates.io API, 2026-10-07): rsntp 4.1.2 MIT OR Apache-2.0 (SNTP, sync + tokio async, no NTS); sntpc 0.11.0 MIT OR Apache-2.0 (SNTP, no_std/async, no NTS); ntp-proto 1.9.0 Apache-2.0 OR MIT (NTS-KE client, packets, Kalman; unstable API); ntpd 1.9.0 Apache-2.0 OR MIT (daemon); rkik-nts 1.4.0 MIT (high-level NTS client, tokio + rustls, created 2025-11, about 30k downloads); ntp_usg-client 5.0.0 Apache-2.0 OR MIT (NTS, created 2026-02, under 600 downloads); roughenough-client/protocol 2.1.0 Apache-2.0 OR MIT; roughtime 0.2.1 0BSD; rusty_time-* 0.2.0 MIT OR Apache-2.0 (new, NTS, few downloads); chrony-candm GPL-2.0 (control protocol only).
findings.evidence: crates.io /api/v1/crates/<name> responses: max_version, license, created and updated dates, downloads, as listed. ntp-proto lib.rs: 'not intended as a public interface at this time ... not intended to give any stability guarantee. Use at your own risk.'

findings.claim: No crate offers NTS together with a pluggable local clock. rkik-nts takes t1/t4 from SystemTime::now(), which is the OS clock on Windows. sntpc has a NtpTimestampGenerator trait for a custom clock (usable with QPC) but no NTS. rsntp reports offsets against the system clock and warns that clock changes invalidate them. Using QPC with NTS needs a small fork of rkik-nts or a custom client on ntp-proto primitives.
findings.evidence: rkik-nts src/nts_ntp.rs line 386: 'let t1 = SystemTime::now();'; line 585: t1 = self.send_time; lines 71-76 compute theta and rtt from t1..t4; TimeSnapshot exposes system_time, network_time, offset, round_trip_delay, authenticated, stratum. sntpc/src/types.rs line 571: 'pub trait NtpTimestampGenerator { fn init(&mut self); fn timestamp_sec(&self)->u64; fn timestamp_subsec_micros(&self)->u32; ... }'; NtpResult has roundtrip, offset, stratum, leap_indicator, root_delay. rsntp README: 'If the system clock is changed between synchronization and the call to this method, then offset will not be valid anymore'.

findings.claim: The ntpd-rs daemon is packaged for Linux, FreeBSD and macOS only. It disciplines the OS clock (needs privileges), so it is unsuitable to embed in a Windows user-mode app. Only its protocol crate is relevant, and I have not verified that it compiles on Windows.
findings.evidence: docs/guide/installation.md has sections for Linux, FreeBSD and macOS ('no package or installer for macOS'), and none for Windows. code-structure.md: 'clock-steering crate wraps the system calls needed for controlling the system clock'. ntp-proto has #![forbid(unsafe_code)] and depends on tokio, rustls and statime-base, so it is probably portable, but this is unverified.

findings.claim: Cloudflare Workers can't host a UDP NTP endpoint (no UDP in the supported protocols), and Date.now() inside a Worker is frozen to the time of the last I/O. A Workers or WebSocket time endpoint is possible but less precise and of unverified accuracy. A real NTP/NTS server needs a VM; Fly.io GRU UDP, for example, requires a dedicated IPv4 and binding to fly-global-services.
findings.evidence: cloudflare-docs workers/reference/protocols.mdx lists only HTTP/HTTPS, direct TCP (outbound via connect(), inbound 'coming soon'), WebSockets, HTTP/3 and SMTP. security-model.mdx: 'Date.now() returns the time of the last I/O. It does not advance during code execution.' Fly.io docs: UDP needs a dedicated IPv4 and the fly-global-services address.

findings.claim: WebSocket/HTTP time-sync libraries (timesync, clocksy, webtimesync) use NTP-like round trips with filtering. The only accuracy claim found is clocksy's '< 10 ms in a few iterations'. HTTP Date headers have only 1 s resolution.
findings.evidence: npm timesync: sync to a server over HTTP or WebSockets, or among peers over WebRTC. clocksy: 'estimate server time and apply an IIR filter', 'convergence to < 10 ms'. webtimesync: the server returns receive and transmit ms timestamps. No benchmark of timesync was found. The HTTP Date resolution is general knowledge and was not fetched here.

findings.claim: For P2P time pings over WebRTC, an unordered channel with maxRetransmits:0 gives UDP-like delivery. This avoids SCTP retransmission and head-of-line delays that would inflate RTT samples.
findings.evidence: MDN createDataChannel: 'ordered ... Default: true'; maxRetransmits 'only used while in unordered ... mode'. web.dev: 'Setzen Sie für die UDP-Semantik maxRetransmits auf 0 und ordered auf false'.

findings.claim: Even with perfect clocks, two players' POVs won't show the same game event at the same wall-clock instant. Client-side entity interpolation alone renders about 100 ms in the past by default in Source, and it varies per client and game. Clock sync much tighter than a few ms therefore has diminishing returns, and the editor needs a manual offset nudge.
findings.evidence: Valve Developer Community: 'entity interpolation causes a constant view lag of 100 milliseconds by default' (cl_interp 0.1). CS2 (Source 2) may differ. The implication for DuoClip is my inference.

findings.claim: Perceptual references for choosing sync targets: audio–video detectability is about +45 ms (audio early) to −125 ms (ITU-R BT.1359), and EBU R37 allows an end-to-end budget of +40/−60 ms. One video frame is 16.7 ms at 60 fps.
findings.evidence: Secondary summaries of ITU-R BT.1359-1 and EBU R37: 'detectability thresholds of +45 ms to -125 ms'; R37 'end-to-end +40 ms ... to −60 ms; each stage within +5 ms and −15 ms'.

findings.claim: Standard container fields exist for storing wall-clock time with media. ISO BMFF 'prft' (ProducerReferenceTimeBox, ISO/IEC 14496-12 §8.16.5) pairs an NTP timestamp with a media time; FFmpeg writes it with -write_prft wallclock|pts. Matroska DateUTC is signed nanoseconds since 2001-01-01 UTC, not counting leap seconds.
findings.evidence: Epic MP4Boxes FMP4BoxPRFT cites 14496-12:2022 §8.16.5. The FFmpeg movenc commit says the box provides 'relative wall-clock times at which movie fragments were produced'. EBML/Matroska: Date element is 'nanoseconds ... 2001-01-01T00:00:00 UTC'; erratum: 'not counting leap seconds'; Unix offset 978307200 s.

findings.claim: I found no published rate limits or embedding terms for time.cloudflare.com or NTP.br. Cloudflare time services fall under the general Website and Online Services Terms (no 'overburden' use). SNTP guidance commonly cited is: never poll more often than every 15 s, and honor Kiss-o'-Death (RATE/DENY/RSTR).
findings.evidence: Cloudflare time-services ToS points to the general terms, which contain no numeric NTP limits. lwIP: '#error SNTPv4 RFC 4330 enforces a minimum update time of 15 seconds'. coreSNTP maps the KoD codes DENY, RSTR and RATE. I did not verify the RFC 4330 text directly.

design_recommendations: Canonical timescale: every clip, frame and hotkey event is stored as UTC (POSIX nanoseconds, leap seconds not counted) derived from an in-app AppClock. AppClock(q) = ref_utc_ns + (q − ref_qpc)·(1e9/QPF)·(1 + rate_ppb·1e-9). Media timestamps come straight from QPC (WGC SystemRelativeTime, WASAPI pu64QPCPosition). Never use the OS clock for sync. GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime is only a coarse initial guess and a cross-check (warn if the OS clock is off by more than 1 s).

Time sources: NTS-only and non-smearing. Use a.st1, b.st1, c.st1 and d.st1.ntp.br, gps.ntp.br (and gps.ce.ntp.br/Fortaleza when confirmed), plus time.cloudflare.com. At startup, probe all of them and keep the 3–4 with the lowest minimum RTT. Never mix in Google or AWS (they smear); exclude time.windows.com (no NTS, observed errors) and plain pool.ntp.org (no NTS, vendor policy). If NTS-KE (TCP 4460) fails, fall back to unauthenticated NTP to the same servers and flag clips 'unauthenticated'. If UDP 123 is blocked, fall back to our own WebSocket time endpoint and/or P2P only.

Polling schedule: at startup send a chrony-iburst-like burst of 4–8 queries per source about 2 s apart, then poll every 64 s per source (the chrony Internet default). Never poll a public server more than once every 15 s. Honor KoD RATE/DENY, add jitter to poll times, and back off when the app is idle. The load is trivial for 5 friends but must be reviewed (vendor contact) before mass distribution.

Sample filter and estimator, per source: keep about 64 (QPC_t1, QPC_t4, t2, t3) tuples. Reject samples with RTT > 150 ms, RTT > 3× min RTT, or above the 20–30% lowest-RTT quantile (chrony maxdelayquant style). Fit a weighted linear regression of offset vs QPC time (weight ∝ 1/(δ−δmin+ε)²) to get offset and frequency (ppm) with residual σ. Combine sources with an interval-intersection (Marzullo-like) step, then inverse-variance weighting; require ≥2 agreeing NTS sources. A two-state Kalman filter (offset, frequency) like ntpd-rs is a later upgrade.

Uncertainty model: for each source, bound = δmin/2 + server root distance (root_delay/2 + root_dispersion, as in chrony) + 2σ regression residual + |freq_uncertainty|·age_since_last_good_sample. Clock bound = the best agreeing source's bound. Keep both a worst-case 'bound' and a statistical '1σ'. Relative uncertainty between two clips = boundA + boundB (show this) and sqrt(σA² + σB²) (for diagnostics).

Live clock: slew only, never step backwards. Limit corrections to about 500–1000 ppm (0.5–1 ms per second). Allow a step only before the first clip of a session or when the error exceeds 1 s, and in that case start a new clock_epoch_id stored in clip metadata. A forward or backward step must never happen inside a recording.

Retroactive re-mapping (biggest accuracy win): clips store raw QPC timestamps plus the mapping in force at the time. When a clip is saved, and again at export, recompute the mapping for that interval with a two-sided regression over sync samples from before AND after the clip. This uses future samples a live estimator can't see, and the improved mapping is written back to the clip metadata.

Hotkey protocol: the clipper broadcasts {hotkey_utc_ns, uncertainty_ns, clock_epoch_id}, not 'now'. Each peer converts hotkey_utc_ns to its own QPC with its mapping and saves [T−N−margin, T+M+margin], where margin = relative uncertainty + one GOP (1 s keyframe interval), trimmed later in the editor. Message delivery delay then doesn't matter.

P2P refinement during a session: send NTP-style 4-timestamp pings (QPC-stamped) every 1–2 s over a dedicated WebRTC data channel (ordered:false, maxRetransmits:0) on a high-priority thread, with min-RTT filtering and regression as above. Fuse with the global estimate using inverse-variance weights, and raise an alert when |global_diff − p2p_diff| exceeds the combined bounds. For 3–5 peers, solve pairwise offsets by weighted least squares and check loop closure. Note when the path is TURN-relayed (larger bound). Store the P2P measurements in clip metadata.

Offline and holdover: a state machine of SYNCED (bound ≤ 8 ms), DEGRADED, HOLDOVER (no sources; extrapolate with the last frequency; bound grows by freq_uncert·t, e.g. 1 ppm ≈ 3.6 ms/h) and UNSYNCED (no frequency estimate; ±10–100 ppm ≈ 36–360 ms/h). Persist the frequency estimate (ppm), per machine and per boot-QPC frequency, in a driftfile-like store so warm restarts converge quickly. Optionally cache NTS cookies (like chrony's ntsdumpdir). Re-burst after resume from sleep or hibernate and after network changes.

Leap seconds: keep the AppClock continuous (QPC-based) and store utc_tai_offset_s (37) and the server leap indicator with each clip. Use only non-smearing sources. If a leap second ever falls inside a session, treat it like chrony 'leapsecmode ignore/slew': keep the media timeline continuous and re-sync afterwards. None is due before mid-2027 (Bulletin C 72) and abolition is planned by 2035, so keep this minimal.

Security posture: no admin, no system-clock changes, no driver; only outbound UDP 123 and TCP 4460 (plus the existing WebRTC). NTS stops spoofing and tampering. Bound delay attacks with the RTT cap and multi-source agreement. If certificate time validation fails because the OS clock is far off, retry NTS-KE with certificate time checks relaxed only if ≥2 independent sources (e.g. NTP.br and Cloudflare, or a Roughtime signed response) agree within 1 s, mirroring chrony nocerttimecheck.

Crate strategy: (a) fork rkik-nts (MIT) and replace SystemTime::now() at src/nts_ntp.rs:386 and :585 with QPC-based timestamps that expose raw t1..t4, or (b) build a small client on ntp-proto's KeyExchangeClient and packet and NTS primitives pinned to =1.9.0, since its API is unstable. Use sntpc with a custom NtpTimestampGenerator (QPC) for the unauthenticated fallback. Write the discipline/estimator in-house (a few hundred lines). Licenses are permissive (MIT/Apache-2.0). Avoid the ntpd daemon (no Windows build, steers the OS clock).

Own infrastructure (phase 2, optional): a São Paulo VM running ntpd-rs or chrony as an NTS server (synced to NTP.br) plus a WebSocket time endpoint. Use it for fallback, telemetry and rate-limit independence. Don't build it on Cloudflare Workers (no UDP; Date.now() frozen to last I/O). Disable Nagle on the WebSocket and use min-RTT filtering; expect a few ms to about 10 ms.

Clip metadata schema (sidecar JSON, plus container fields: MP4 'prft' or Matroska DateUTC set from AppClock, not the OS clock). Fields: clip_id, session_id, participant_id, timescale='utc_posix_ns', clock_epoch_id, start_utc_ns, end_utc_ns, hotkey_utc_ns, uncertainty_bound_ns, uncertainty_sigma_ns, sync_state, qpc_frequency, start_qpc, mapping{ref_qpc, ref_utc_ns, rate_ppb, method:'live'|'two_sided'}, sources[{host, ip, nts:bool, stratum, min_rtt_us, samples, root_distance_us}], last_sync_age_ms, peer_offsets[{peer_id, offset_ns, bound_ns, rtt_us, path:'direct'|'turn'}], utc_tai_offset_s, leap_indicator, os_clock_offset_ms (diagnostic).

UI and uncertainty display: lobby badge per friend, e.g. 'Relógio global: ±3 ms (NTS ✓)'. Green when the pairwise bound is ≤ 8 ms (half a frame at 60 fps), yellow up to 33 ms (≤ 2 frames), red above that or HOLDOVER/UNSYNCED. In the editor, show the alignment uncertainty bracket on the timeline and offer a manual nudge (±500 ms, 1-frame and 1-ms steps), because netcode interpolation (~100 ms in Source) shifts on-screen events between POVs. Optionally add audio cross-correlation, e.g. of a third friend's Discord voice heard on both PCs, or of shared game sounds, for fine alignment.

Validation and telemetry: log per-user anonymised min-RTT, bound distribution, ISP type (fiber, Wi-Fi, 4G) and global-vs-P2P disagreement to get real Brazilian numbers, since none were found publicly. Add a 'sync test' mode where both PCs record a shared on-screen event, for example a round start or a time.is page, to measure the actual end-to-end offset.

Does NTP.br leap-smear? Assumed not, but not verified.

research.topic: Cloud object-storage bucket for temporary DuoClip clip exchange (R2 vs Supabase vs S3 sa-east-1 vs B2 vs Wasabi vs GCS southamerica-east1), expiry/TTL, upload mechanisms, security/LGPD, cost for 1,000 users, and P2P-vs-bucket architecture (plus local segmented "time-bucket" disk buffer)
research.summary: Cloudflare R2 is the clear cost winner for temporary clip exchange. Its egress is free on every storage class, Standard storage costs $0.015/GB-month, Class A operations $4.50/M, Class B $0.36/M, and DeleteObject and AbortMultipartUpload cost nothing. The free tier gives 10 GB-month, 1M Class A and 10M Class B per month. At the target load (1,000 users x 20 clips x 60 MB = 1.2 TB uploaded and about 1.2 TB downloaded per month, 72 h retention, about 120 GB-month stored), R2 costs about $1.65-$2.25/month, or about $3.6-$4.3 with no free tier. For the same load, S3 sa-east-1 costs about $173 (egress $0.15/GB after a 100 GB global free allowance), GCS southamerica-east1 about $148 (egress $0.12/GB), Supabase Pro about $111 ($25 base + $0.09/GB uncached egress beyond 250 GB), and Backblaze B2 about $9 (free egress up to 3x stored volume; secondary sources). Wasabi does not fit this use. Each object is billed for at least 90 days (about 3.6 TB billed at steady state, roughly $25-$29/month), its free-egress policy assumes egress no larger than stored volume, and it has no South American region (secondary sources). R2 has no South America location hint; the hints are wnam, enam, weur, eeur, apac and oc. Cloudflare's own docs map AWS sa-east-1 to hint enam, so R2 data for Brazilian users would sit in Eastern North America. R2 'Local Uploads' (open beta since 2026-02-03, no extra cost) writes data near the client and replicates it asynchronously. Cloudflare reports up to 75% lower upload TTLB, but I could not confirm whether there is South American storage behind it. São Paulo data residency is available from S3 sa-east-1, GCS southamerica-east1 and Supabase sa-east-1 (which runs on AWS São Paulo), at roughly 50-100x the R2 cost because egress dominates. Native expiry is day-granular everywhere: R2 lifecycle Days or Date (objects removed typically within 24 h after expiration, billed until deleted); S3 Days rounded up to the next midnight UTC (not billed after expiration); GCS age in days (rule changes take up to 24 h, and soft delete keeps deleted objects for 7 days by default, billed as storage); B2 at least 1 day to hide plus at least 1 day hidden-to-delete. Supabase Storage has no current-object expiry: its new bucket lifecycle API only supports noncurrentVersionExpiration and rejects current-object expiration. TTL there needs pg_cron or a scheduled Edge Function calling the Storage API remove() (deleting via SQL orphans the files). Expiry measured in hours therefore always needs app-driven deletion, with lifecycle rules kept only as a backstop. Desktop clients can upload without long-lived keys in two ways on R2: presigned PUT/GET/HEAD/DELETE URLs valid from 1 s to 7 days (POST form uploads are not supported), or temporary credentials scoped to a bucket, a set of actions and path prefixes, with ttlSeconds and local JWT minting. On Supabase the options are TUS resumable uploads (6 MB chunks, upload URL valid up to 24 h), createSignedUploadUrl (valid 2 h), createSignedUrl downloads and RLS on storage.objects. For security, encrypt each clip end-to-end on the client with AES-256-GCM and a per-clip key that goes only to the paired friend. Encrypt in independent chunks so ranges can be fetched, which also keeps the provider from reading the clips and reduces LGPD exposure. Storing on R2 ENAM is an international transfer under LGPD Art. 33, so the privacy notice and the legal basis must cover it; I could not fetch the law text in this session. My recommendation is bucket-first on R2 with progressive, encrypted, chunked uploads and opportunistic P2P for the 720p proxy, rather than P2P-first. Bucket-first works when the friend is offline or behind NAT, lets the uploading PC finish fast, and costs almost nothing. A local segmented disk 'time bucket' (1-2 s keyframe-aligned segments indexed by the global clock) complements this: it is useful for long buffers, for crash resilience and for serving arbitrary global-clock time ranges. OBS itself keeps its replay buffer as an in-RAM packet deque. Note: the web-search budget for this run ran out near the end, so the Wasabi, B2 and LGPD items could not be re-checked against official pages.

findings.claim: R2 Standard storage pricing: $0.015/GB-month storage, Class A $4.50/million, Class B $0.36/million, egress free; Infrequent Access is $0.01/GB-month but has a 30-day minimum storage duration and $0.01/GB retrieval fees, so it is unsuitable for 24-72 h clips.
findings.evidence: R2 pricing table: 'Storage $0.015 / GB-month | $0.01 / GB-month', 'Class A Operations $4.50 / million requests', 'Class B Operations $0.36 / million requests', 'Egress (data transfer to Internet) Free'; 'Minimum storage duration: Standard storage None; Infrequent Access storage 30 days'. Read from cloudflare-docs source src/content/docs/r2/pricing.mdx lines 30-36 and 95-98 (commit 31febb14, 2026-10-07).

findings.claim: R2 free tier (Standard only): 10 GB-month storage, 1 million Class A, 10 million Class B per month. DeleteObject, DeleteBucket and AbortMultipartUpload are free. Usage rounds up to the next billing unit. Storage GB-month is the average of the daily PEAK storage. Requests rejected as unauthorized (401) are not billed.
findings.evidence: pricing.mdx lines 52-57 (free tier table), line 85 'Free operations include DeleteObject, DeleteBucket and AbortMultipartUpload', line 65 'averaging the _peak_ storage per day over a billing period (30 days)', lines 38-45 rounding, line 171 'You are not charged for operations when the caller does not have permission to make the request (HTTP 401...)'.

findings.claim: R2 lifecycle rules support Expiration by Days or Date, transition to IA, and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload (DaysAfterInitiation), with prefix filters and up to 1,000 rules. Granularity is whole days. Deletion is typically within 24 h after the x-amz-expiration time, and storage is billed until the object is actually deleted. Buckets have a default rule that aborts multipart uploads after 7 days.
findings.evidence: object-lifecycles.mdx: 'Objects will typically be removed from a bucket within 24 hours of the x-amz-expiration value'; 'An object is no longer billable once it has been deleted'; 'Buckets have a default lifecycle rule to expire multipart uploads seven days after initiation'; 'object lifecycles currently has a 1000 rule maximum'; examples use Expiration: { Days: 90 } and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload: { DaysAfterInitiation: 1 }.

findings.claim: R2 has no South America location hint and no Brazilian jurisdiction. Hints are wnam, enam, weur, eeur, apac and oc; jurisdictions are eu, fedramp and us. Automatic placement picks the 'closest available region' to the bucket-creation request. Cloudflare's own mapping recommends hint 'enam' for AWS South America (São Paulo).
findings.evidence: data-location.mdx hint table (wnam, enam, weur, eeur, apac, oc) and jurisdiction table (eu, fedramp, us); 'chooses a bucket location in the closest available region to the create bucket request'. partners/snowflake-regions.mdx line 24: 'South America (Sao Paulo) | AWS | sa-east-1 | Location hint: enam'.

findings.claim: R2 Local Uploads (open beta since 2026-02-03, no extra cost) writes PutObject/UploadPart data to storage near the client, replicates it asynchronously to the bucket's region, and keeps the object immediately readable and strongly consistent. Cloudflare reports up to 75% lower upload time-to-last-byte. It is not available on jurisdiction-restricted buckets. Reads from near the bucket region may see cross-region latency until replication finishes.
findings.evidence: buckets/local-uploads.mdx: 'Object data is written to storage near the client, then asynchronously replicated to your bucket. The object is immediately accessible and remains durable'; 'Local uploads are not supported for buckets with jurisdictional restrictions'; 'There is no additional cost'. changelog/r2/2026-02-03-r2-local-uploads.mdx: 'up to 75% reduction in Time to Last Byte (TTLB)'.

findings.claim: R2 presigned URLs support GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE with expiry from 1 second to 7 days. POST form uploads (with policy conditions such as content-length-range) are not supported. Content-Type can be signed, so a mismatched upload fails with 403. Presigned URLs only work on the S3 API domain, not on custom domains.

findings.claim: R2 temporary credentials are short-lived SigV4 credentials with a session token. Each is bound to one bucket and a permission scope or action list, and can be restricted to path prefixes or exact objects with a ttlSeconds lifetime. They can be minted through Cloudflare's API or locally by signing an HS256 JWT with the parent secret, and action-level scoping is supported only through local signing. This lets a desktop client run standard S3 multipart uploads without holding long-lived keys.

Set ttlSeconds...'. The example in examples/authenticate-r2-temp-credentials.mdx uses ttlSeconds 900 (default 3600 in its helper).

findings.claim: R2 multipart constraints: parts must be 5 MiB-5 GiB (the last part may be smaller), at most 10,000 parts, and all parts except the last must be the same size. Single PUT allows up to 5 GiB. A pipelined 'download while uploading' design therefore needs separate chunk objects (a multipart object can only be read after CompleteMultipartUpload; that last point is standard S3 semantics, inferred).

findings.claim: R2 encrypts objects at rest with AES-256-GCM using Cloudflare-managed keys, and supports SSE-C (customer-provided keys). Both are server-side, so Cloudflare handles the plaintext or key. Client-side E2E encryption is still needed if the provider must never be able to read clips.
