findings.claim: OBS's replay buffer is an in-memory deque of encoded packets, trimmed from the front by max_time_sec and max_size_mb. It always purges whole GOPs (up to the next video keyframe) and keeps at least 2 keyframes. This is a RAM ring rather than a disk 'time-bucket' buffer, and it confirms the current plan (RAM ring of encoded packets with a 1 s keyframe interval) matches OBS's design.
findings.evidence: obs-studio plugins/obs-ffmpeg/obs-ffmpeg-mux.c (commit 39c2de97, 2026-10-07): replay_buffer_start reads 'max_time_sec' and 'max_size_mb' (lines ~973-974); purge_front() does deque_pop_front(&stream->packets...); purge() keeps purging until the next 'pkt.type == OBS_ENCODER_VIDEO && pkt.keyframe'; replay_buffer_purge() returns early if 'stream->keyframes <= 2' (lines ~984-1043).

findings.claim: A local segmented disk buffer ('time buckets' of 1-2 s keyframe-aligned fMP4/MPEG-TS segments named by global-clock start time) is useful in four cases: very long buffers (minutes) without large RAM use; crash and restart resilience; serving any [t0, t1] global-clock range to the friend; and progressive upload, since each sealed segment can be encrypted and uploaded while post-roll is still recording. Costs: continuous SSD writes (about 22.5 GB/hour at 50 Mbps, 6.25 MB/s) and the need to encrypt or clean temp files. A hybrid (RAM ring for the last N seconds, spill to disk segments only when the buffer setting is long) avoids constant disk writes for default short buffers.
findings.evidence: Design reasoning; bitrate arithmetic 50 Mbit/s / 8 = 6.25 MB/s x 3600 s = 22.5 GB/h. The OBS RAM design is from the finding above. Medal and ShadowPlay buffer internals were not researched in this task.

findings.claim: LGPD considerations. Gameplay video and especially Discord voice of the user and third parties are personal data. Storing clips on R2 (ENAM, USA) or any non-Brazil region is an international data transfer that needs an Art. 33 mechanism, such as the ANPD standard contractual clauses (Resolução CD/ANPD nº 19/2024) or specific consent. Data should be deleted when processing ends (Art. 16), data subjects have a deletion right (Art. 18), and security measures (Art. 46) and incident notification (Art. 48) apply. Client-side E2E encryption with keys held only by the paired friends, short retention and verifiable deletion materially lower breach risk and impact. A São Paulo region avoids the transfer question but not the other duties.

findings.claim: Expiry granularity summary: hour-level TTL is impossible natively on all compared providers. R2: Days or Date, then up to about 24 h removal delay, billed until deletion. findings.claim: Architecture comparison. Bucket-first works when the friend is offline or closed the app, when NAT traversal fails (no TURN relay needed for file transfer), and asynchronously. It lets the uploading PC finish as soon as its upstream allows and gives a single resumable path (multipart or TUS). Costs: data crosses BR to US to BR on R2 (two long hops), there is some extra time-to-first-byte, and you rely on a third-party store. P2P-first gives the lowest latency when both peers are online in Brazil, and storage and egress cost nothing on a direct path. But WebRTC file transfer must handle NAT failure (TURN relays also cost egress), both apps must stay open, and resume logic is more complex. Because R2 makes bucket egress free, the cost argument for P2P mostly disappears; it stays relevant for S3, GCS or Supabase, where 70% P2P success cuts the bill about 4x.
findings.evidence: Design reasoning built on the cost figures above. TURN pricing was not researched.

design_recommendations: Use Cloudflare R2 as the default temporary clip store, bucket-first. At the target load it costs about $2-4/month for 1,000 users because egress is free, versus about $110-175/month on São Paulo providers. Turn on R2 Local Uploads (free, beta) and benchmark from real Brazilian ISPs. Never use R2 Infrequent Access, S3-IA or GCS Nearline for clips, because of their 30-day minimums.

Upload progressively, in encrypted chunk objects. When the hotkey is pressed, the friend's app immediately uploads the pre-roll segments from the ring or disk buffer, then the post-roll segments as each 1-2 s keyframe-aligned segment seals. Group segments into about 4-8 MiB chunk objects named clips/{pairId}/{clipId}/{pov}/{quality}/{chunkIdx} plus an encrypted manifest that maps chunk to global-clock time range. Separate objects, rather than multipart parts, let the clipper download chunk N while chunk N+1 is still uploading. Multipart objects can only be read after Complete, and R2 requires equal-size parts.

Send the 720p proxy first, so the clipper's editor can show both POVs within seconds. Then upload full-quality chunks only for the trimmed [start, end] range that the clipper selects. The selection is sent over the authenticated channel and mapped to chunk indices using global-clock timestamps.

Use client-side end-to-end encryption. The uploader generates a random 256-bit key per clip and encrypts each chunk with AES-256-GCM, using a unique 96-bit nonce (random prefix plus chunk counter) and AAD = clipId|pov|quality|chunkIdx|isLast. The AAD prevents swapping, reordering and truncation. The per-clip key goes only to the paired friend over the authenticated WebRTC data channel or app channel. A vetted streaming-AEAD construction (e.g. libsodium secretstream or Tink AES-GCM-HKDF streaming) is an alternative to hand-rolling. The storage provider then only ever holds ciphertext.

Never ship long-lived bucket keys in the desktop app. A small backend (a Cloudflare Worker next to R2) authenticates the user, checks that the requester belongs to the pair or session for that clipId, and returns either (a) R2 temporary credentials scoped to that prefix with ttlSeconds of about 900 and only the needed actions, or (b) per-object presigned PUT/GET URLs with expiry of 15 minutes or less and a signed Content-Type. Downloads use presigned GET URLs issued only to the paired friend.

Delete clips from the app and keep lifecycle rules as a backstop. Use explicit DeleteObject (free on R2) once the clipper confirms export or rejects the clip, plus an hourly scheduled sweeper (Worker cron) that enforces the 24-72 h TTL to the hour from a clip registry (D1/KV/DB row with expires_at). Also add an R2 lifecycle rule on prefix clips/ with Expiration Days = 3 (or 4) and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload of 1 day for crash leftovers.

Rate-limit and cap abuse in the credential-minting Worker. Enforce per-user quotas (bytes/day, active clips, maximum chunk size and count per clip, e.g. at most 120 s x 60 Mbps), let only paired friends get read URLs, and use short TTLs. R2 does not bill 401 requests, but valid-credential abuse is billable for Class A operations, so the quotas matter. Log uploads per user.

Keep P2P (WebRTC) as an opportunistic accelerator, not the primary transport. When both peers are online with a direct (non-TURN) path, send the proxy and preview over the data channel and let the clipper take each chunk from whichever source delivers it first. If the friend goes offline, NAT fails or a TURN relay would be needed, the bucket path already has the data. Under this design a TURN relay is never needed for file transfer.

If Brazilian data residency becomes a hard requirement, use S3 sa-east-1 (consider CloudFront in front for 1 TB/month of free egress; CloudFront pricing beyond that was not verified) or Supabase Pro in sa-east-1. Budget about $110-175/month per 1,000 users at this volume, or about $35-41 with P2P handling 70%. With GCS southamerica-east1, disable soft delete on the temp bucket. Avoid Wasabi (90-day minimum billing, egress policy, no SA region) and treat B2 as a cheap non-Brazil alternative (US/EU/CA only).

If Supabase is chosen: Pro plan (Free caps files at 50 MB); TUS resumable uploads with 6 MB chunks or createSignedUploadUrl (valid 2 h); RLS on storage.objects so INSERT is allowed only under the uploader's own uid folder and SELECT only where a pairing table (clip_shares) contains auth.uid(); a pg_cron or scheduled Edge Function that deletes through the Storage API remove() (max 1,000 per call, never via SQL); a Spend Cap to block runaway egress; reuse of one signed URL per download session to improve CDN hits.

Local buffer: keep the OBS-style in-RAM ring of encoded packets (1 s GOP) as the default. Add an optional disk 'time-bucket' mode, with 1-2 s segments named by global-clock start time, for long buffers, crash resilience and serving exact global-clock ranges to the friend. Make it a user setting because of SSD writes (about 22.5 GB/h at 50 Mbps), and encrypt or wipe the segment files.

LGPD: disclose international storage (if R2/US) in the privacy policy and rely on the provider's contractual clauses (verify ANPD Res. 19/2024 SCC compatibility). Get consent and notice for capturing friends' Discord voice. Keep retention to the minimum (delete after export, hard limit 72 h), provide in-app 'delete my clips now', and log deletions. Note that E2E encryption with user-held keys strongly limits breach impact.

Actual clip sizes: is ~60 MB per POV the full window (N+M seconds at what bitrate)? How big is the 720p proxy? Are both directions transferred (each friend's POV to the other) or only the friend's POV to the clipper? Any of these could double the upload and egress volumes.
Maximum ttlSeconds allowed for R2 temporary credentials was not found in the docs.
Whether a TURN relay would be needed for the P2P path, and what it costs (e.g. Cloudflare Realtime TURN or self-hosted coturn egress), was not researched.

research.topic: Recording beyond the press time: post-roll, pinning, safety margins, RAM vs disk-segment buffers, and two-PC finalization for a replay-buffer clipper (DuoClip)
research.summary:
The OBS replay buffer only saves the past. In the OBS source, the save hotkey just records the press time as save_ts using os_gettime_ns(), which is based on QueryPerformanceCounter (QPC) on Windows. The file is cut when the first encoded packet with sys_dts_usec >= save_ts arrives, so the end is the press moment and there is no post-roll. That same mechanism also absorbs encoder latency, which is the pattern DuoClip should copy: wait until every track has emitted packets past the target end.

OBS keeps the range from being evicted by taking refcounted copies of the buffered packets (obs_encoder_packet_ref) into a separate mux list, written on its own thread, while the RAM ring keeps running. The ring evicts whole GOPs and always keeps at least 2 keyframes. OBS has no built-in post-roll. Forum users ask for it, and the workarounds are delayed saves via script timers, Stream Deck multi-actions, or buffer restart scripts.

The only tool found with an explicit past+future API is Overwolf, the platform under Outplayed: capture(pastDuration, futureDuration, captureFinishedCallback). Its docs say the buffer is held "in the memory" and allow only one capture at a time. A forum report says pastDuration is capped at about 180 s. Outplayed exposes before/after sliders per game.

Medal, NVIDIA Instant Replay, AMD Instant Replay, Xbox Game Bar and SteelSeries Moments all save only past footage for the clip hotkey. For later footage they offer long recordings, bookmarks or hold-to-record instead; no "seconds after" option was found. Steam Game Recording avoids the problem: it keeps a disk-capped background recording, reportedly DASH .m4s segments plus a session.mpd, and the user drags clip start and end anywhere on the timeline, including after the moment. Steamworks' timeline API even says suggested clips for instant events cover "a short time before and after the event".

The industry splits on storage. OBS and Overwolf buffer in RAM. NVIDIA (a "Temporary files location" setting), AMD (hard drive by default, optional system memory) and Steam (disk segments) buffer on disk.

Recommended design: a RAM ring of encoded packets in local QPC time, and a two-phase "pin then collect" clip state machine. When the request arrives, take references to everything from the keyframe at or before the start. Keep appending live packets until all tracks pass the end plus margin, or a timeout fires. Meanwhile, stream the clip into a crash-safe fragmented MP4 in a local per-clip "bucket" folder, so a crash or game exit during post-roll still leaves a decodable file (both FFmpeg's docs and OBS's Hybrid MP4 muxer rely on this).

Forcing a keyframe is not needed for stream-copy cuts with a fixed 1 s GOP; extend the window outward to GOP boundaries instead. Forced-IDR APIs exist on all three vendors (NVENC NV_ENC_PIC_FLAG_FORCEIDR, AMF ForcePictureType/Av1ForceFrameType, oneVPL mfxEncodeCtrl.FrameType=IDR) and in Media Foundation (CODECAPI_AVEncVideoForceKeyFrame).

For two PCs, every request carries a clip_id and the press time in the app's shared global clock, matching the user's request not to rely on the PC clock. Each PC converts that time to its own QPC with the offset frozen at request time, pins on arrival, and finalizes at global T+M+margin. A late request still works while the ring holds the start. If it doesn't, the PC returns a partial clip with coverage metadata instead of failing. Proposed defaults: pre 30 s, post 10 s, hidden margins of 2 s on each side, 1 s closed GOP with no B-frames, a 60 s RAM ring, finalize timeout of end+3 s, and a 180 s cap per clip including extensions.

findings.claim: OBS native replay buffer captures only footage BEFORE the save hotkey: the save proc stores the current monotonic time and the file is cut at the first encoded packet whose system DTS reaches that time (no post-roll). This also means OBS waits for encoder pipeline latency before cutting.
findings.evidence: save_replay_proc(): `stream->save_ts = os_gettime_ns() / 1000LL;` (obs-ffmpeg-mux.c L917-932). replay_buffer_data(): `if (stream->save_ts && packet->sys_dts_usec >= stream->save_ts) { ... stream->save_ts = 0; replay_buffer_save(stream); }` (L1194-1239, check at L1227). OBS commit 39c2de975bb94058553fe8da85cb991c28b37202.

findings.claim: OBS's clock for these timestamps is QPC on Windows, and libobs deliberately stamps all encoder packets with system time so different encoders (video/audio) stay in sync — i.e., one monotonic shared timebase, not wall-clock time.
findings.evidence: platform-windows.c os_gettime_ns(): `QueryPerformanceCounter(&current_time); return util_mul_div64(current_time.QuadPart, 1000000000, get_clockfreq());` (L391-396). obs-encoder.c: `/* we use system time here to ensure sync with other encoders, you do not want to use relative timestamps here */ pkt->dts_usec = encoder->start_ts / 1000 + packet_dts_usec(pkt) - encoder->offset_usec; pkt->sys_dts_usec = pkt->dts_usec;` (~L1405-1414).

findings.claim: OBS RAM ring evicts whole GOPs from the front (never leaving a partial GOP at the head) and always keeps at least 2 keyframes; limits are time (max_time_sec) and size (max_size_mb). Plugin defaults are 15 s / 500 MB; frontend defaults are 20 s / 512 MB.
findings.evidence: purge(): after popping a keyframe, keeps popping until the next video keyframe (L1015-1029). replay_buffer_purge(): `if (!stream->packets.size || stream->keyframes <= 2) return; while ((pkt->dts_usec - stream->cur_time) > stream->max_time) purge(stream);` (L1031-1045). replay_buffer_defaults: max_time_sec 15, max_size_mb 500 (L1241-1245). OBSBasic.cpp: `RecRBTime`, 20 / `RecRBSize`, 512 (L642-643, L685-686).

findings.claim: OBS 'pins' the saved range by taking refcounted references of every buffered packet into a separate list (re-based timestamps, re-sorted by dts_usec for A/V interleave) and muxes it on a separate thread, so the live ring keeps evicting without affecting the save. A second save request while muxing is still running is not dropped: save_ts stays set and the save happens on the first packet after muxing ends (so it ends later than the press).
findings.evidence: insert_packet(): `obs_encoder_packet_ref(&pkt, packet);` then inserts sorted by dts_usec (L1048-1073). replay_buffer_save() copies all packets then `pthread_create(&stream->mux_thread, NULL, replay_buffer_mux_thread, stream)` (L1125-1178). In replay_buffer_data: `if (os_atomic_load_bool(&stream->muxing)) return;` happens before `stream->save_ts = 0` (L1227-1236).

findings.claim: OBS has no built-in option for N seconds after the hotkey. Users have asked for it repeatedly. Community workarounds are a longer buffer trimmed later, delayed saves (a script timer or Stream Deck multi-action), and save-stop-start restart scripts, which mainly prevent clip overlap and lose about 1 s per save.
findings.evidence: Forum thread 'Replay buffer - record after hotkey': a user wants time before and after the press in one file and reports nothing in OBS 27.1.3 or plugins does it. Thread 28002 'Can replay buffer record X seconds after pushing hotkey?': the reply suggests a longer buffer plus trimming. 'Smarter Replay Buffer Options?': the restart approach can lose about 1 s after every save. GitHub Shabure/obs-sequential-replay-control: 'save, stop, and start replay buffer with a single hotkey'. ItsLeMax/Replay-Restarter: restarts 'to prevent clip overlapping'. Advanced Scene Switcher has wait and replay-buffer save actions that could build a delayed save; a 2022 user reported saves failing if issued within about 15 s of each other. Forum pages were seen only through search excerpts, because obsproject.com was blocked from this environment.

findings.claim: OBS's 'Replay Source' plugin (exeldro) is an in-memory replay-for-playback filter (Duration, Load delay, Maximum replays), not a post-roll clip saver. Elgato's OBS instant-replay widget uses separate Start/End hotkeys (behavior not verified).
findings.evidence: README: '(async) replay filter Keeps the configured seconds from a source in memory' with properties Duration / Load delay / Maximum replays. Elgato docs: assign hotkeys for the widget's Start and End functions (seen via search excerpt).

findings.claim: Overwolf (the platform under Outplayed) has a native replay API with explicit past and future durations. Its buffer is in memory, only one capture can be written at a time, and an open-ended start/stop variant exists.
findings.evidence: overwolf.d.ts: turnOn(): 'buffer_length defines the amount of time in milliseconds to have captured in the memory at all times' (L873-886). capture(pastDuration, futureDuration, captureFinishedCallback, callback): 'pastDuration The replay length, in milliseconds to include prior to the time of this call. futureDuration ... to include after the time of this call ... captureFinishedCallback ... called when capturing is finished, at the end of the future duration' and 'You can only call this method if replay mode is on and no other replay is currently being captured to a file' (L905-928). startCapture(pastDuration)/stopCapture(replayId) give open-ended capture (L953-1010).

findings.claim: Overwolf replays are meant for short highlights: a developer reported pastDuration over 180000 ms produced clips of about 180 s, and staff said anything over 3 min is not 'short'. The ow-electron recorder's captureReplay uses pastDuration plus an optional timeout instead of futureDuration; per the docs, timeout 0 includes only the past segment.
findings.evidence: Forum thread title 'Overwolf.media.replays.capture() with pastDuration parameter set to greater than 180000 doesn't work'. The staff reply ('180000 ms is 3 minutes, and anything longer is not considered short') and the ow-electron CaptureReplayOptions description were seen only via search excerpts; dev.overwolf.com was blocked here.

findings.claim: Outplayed lets users set seconds BEFORE and AFTER each detected game event (per game, Advanced Options sliders) for Highlights mode; Full Match/Full Session modes record whole matches/sessions with events bookmarked. Default/max slider values not found.
findings.evidence: allthings.how guide: 'Advanced Options' shows 'a few sliders that control the duration of the video capture before and after the event'. The Outplayed privacy policy mentions configurable highlight 'tail durations'. Overwolf support describes per-game capture modes. Seen via search excerpts only.

findings.claim: Medal's clip hotkey saves only past footage; reported presets include 15, 30, 45, 60 and 120 s, longer options up to 20 min, and a 30 s default. For footage after a moment, Medal offers Long Recording or 'Hold to Record', where the clip key becomes a bookmark key. A user feature request asks for a clip hotkey that records from the clip point onward, suggesting no native post-roll at the time.
findings.evidence: Medal help center, as quoted by search: with clip length 30 s, 'only the past 30 seconds of video will be saved'; Clip Capture saves the previous 15/30/45/60/120 s, with longer times up to 20 min. Medal settings article: Clip Length. Long recording: the clip key acts as a bookmark; clips from a session are up to 2 min (10 min with Premium). nolt #169 requests 'starting a recording from the clip point onward'; nolt #92 comment notes 'Hold to Record' under Settings > Hotkeys. support.medal.tv was blocked here, so this comes from search excerpts.

findings.claim: NVIDIA Instant Replay saves only the last N seconds or minutes before the hotkey (Alt+F10). Its buffer appears to be disk-backed: there is a user-settable 'Temporary files location', and GeForce Experience 1.8.2 added an option to move the ShadowPlay buffer directory. If that drive fills, buffering stops.
findings.evidence: NVIDIA ShadowPlay page: 'hit a hotkey to save the last 30 seconds of gameplay'. Third-party guides: the overlay settings include 'Temporary files location', described as where ShadowPlay keeps the initial Instant Replay buffer, and buffering halts when the drive fills (BGR). LegitReviews: GFE 1.8.2 'option to change the directory of the ShadowPlay buffer'. No post-roll option was found.

findings.claim: AMD Adrenalin Instant Replay is past-only. Its buffer is reportedly on the hard drive by default and can be switched to system memory; buffers of up to 20 minutes are reported.
findings.evidence: Overclockers forum (2020 drivers): 'instant replay buffer by default it's set to hard drive but it can be changed to system memory'. A Steam beta discussion from Nov 2024 confirms the save-to-memory option. Evetech guide: up to 20 minutes. No post-roll option was found.

findings.claim: Xbox Game Bar 'Record what happened' (Win+Alt+G) is past-only, with a buffer of 15 s to 10 min (30 s default). It is a separate setting from the 'Record this' maximum length.
findings.evidence: Technipages and Laptop Mag list choices from 15 s to 10 min; Thurrott names a 30 s default; Elevenforum documents the toggle. No Microsoft page was retrieved.

findings.claim: Steam Game Recording avoids post-roll entirely. Background recording is a disk-space-capped rolling recording (reported as about 2 h), and the user picks any start and end on the timeline later, including time after the moment. On disk it is reportedly stored as fragmented MPEG-DASH: many .m4s chunks plus a session.mpd per recording.
findings.evidence: Steam Support (via search excerpt): you choose 'the maximum amount of space on your hard drive'; recordings 'will be overwritten as you play'; 'The Clip button will drop a clip suggestion on the timeline that you can adjust by dragging the end points, or using the Start and End Clip buttons.' Shacknews: '120 minutes of footage'. Steam community: each recording folder has 'a lot of files ... most of them .m4s', and players open session.mpd. A 2024 beta request for a 'last X seconds' hotkey implies it did not exist then.

findings.claim: Steamworks Timeline API (Valve SDK) lets games place events at negative or positive offsets from 'now'. For instant events, Steam's suggested clip covers a short time BEFORE AND AFTER the event, which is Valve's built-in pre+post padding concept.
findings.evidence: ISteamTimeline doc comment (mirrored in Steamworks.NET autogen): 'flStartOffsetSeconds: The time that this range started relative to now. Negative times indicate an event that happened in the past.' and 'ePossibleClip: ... For instantaneous events, the suggested clip will be for a short time before and after the event itself.' Functions include AddInstantaneousTimelineEvent, AddRangeTimelineEvent, StartRangeTimelineEvent and EndRangeTimelineEvent(flEndOffsetSeconds).

findings.claim: SteelSeries Moments: no 'seconds after' or after-event setting was found. Manual (Alt+S) and auto-clips use the default clip duration (reported as 30 s to 5 min), and the editor trims start and end.
findings.evidence: SteelSeries blog posts: Auto-clip tab with per-game triggers; a Clips page sets the default duration, quality, resolution and FPS; 'previous 30 seconds up to 5-minute long clips'. Not found: any post-roll control.

findings.claim: Force-keyframe APIs exist for all target encoders. NVENC: per-picture NV_ENC_PIC_FLAG_FORCEIDR in encodePicFlags, valid only when enablePTD=1; GOP via gopLength/idrPeriod. AMD AMF: per-submission ForcePictureType=IDR (H.264), HevcForcePictureType (HEVC), Av1ForceFrameType=KEY (AV1). Intel oneVPL/QSV: per-frame mfxEncodeCtrl.FrameType with MFX_FRAMETYPE_IDR. Media Foundation: CODECAPI_AVEncVideoForceKeyFrame, applying to the next input frame.
findings.evidence: nvEncodeAPI.h: `NV_ENC_PIC_FLAG_FORCEIDR = 0x2, /**< Encode the current picture as an IDR picture. This flag is only valid when Picture type decision is taken by the Encoder [_NV_ENC_INITIALIZE_PARAMS::enablePTD == 1]. */` (L684-686); gopLength (L2203); idrPeriod (L1867). VideoEncoderVCE.h: '// Per-submission properties - can be set on input surface interface ... AMF_VIDEO_ENCODER_FORCE_PICTURE_TYPE L"ForcePictureType"' (L288-291), enum ... PICTURE_TYPE_IDR (L127-130). VideoEncoderHEVC.h L257. VideoEncoderAV1.h: FORCE_FRAME_TYPE_KEY=1 (L108-111); Av1ForceFrameType (L304); GOP 'may be interrupted by AMF_VIDEO_ENCODER_AV1_FORCE_FRAME_TYPE' (L281). mfxstructures.h mfxEncodeCtrl.FrameType: 'If the encoder works in the display order, only key frames are enforceable.' (L2881-2886); MFX_FRAMETYPE_IDR=0x0080 (L2990). MS docs: 'If the value is nonzero, the encoder will code the next frame as a key frame ... The setting resets to zero after the next frame.'

findings.claim: Hardware encoders return packets later than the frame time: NVENC may buffer input frames for B-frame reordering (and for lookahead), so packets for time T arrive several frames later. The clip finalizer must wait for output timestamps, not wall-clock time.
findings.evidence: nvEncodeAPI.h NV_ENC_ERR_NEED_MORE_INPUT: 'This indicates encode driver requires more input buffers to produce an output bitstream ... If the client is encoding with B frames then, ::NvEncEncodePicture() API might be buffering the input frame for re-ordering.' (L603-617); enableLookahead: 'input frames must remain available to the encoder until encode completion' (L1584).

findings.claim: Fragmented MP4 written incrementally stays decodable if writing is interrupted (crash, power loss). OBS's own MP4 muxer, used for its Hybrid MP4 output, cuts a fragment at each video keyframe only after ALL tracks have caught up to that keyframe's PTS (an A/V interleave wait). On a clean stop it writes a full moov and rewrites the header into a normal MP4.
findings.evidence: FFmpeg muxers doc: 'Writing a fragmented file has the advantage that the file is decodable even if the writing is interrupted (while a normal MOV/MP4 is undecodable if it is not properly finished), and it requires less memory when writing very long files' (L407-413); movflag 'frag_keyframe: start a new fragment at each video keyframe' (L536-537). OBS mp4-mux.c: `fragment_ready = fragment_ready && tmp->last_pts_usec >= mux->next_frag_pts;` ... `/* If all tracks have caught up to the keyframe we want to fragment on, flush the current fragment to disk. */` (L2900-2938); mp4_mux_finalise flushes the final fragment, then 'Write full moov box' and 'Overwrite file header (ftyp + free/moov)' (L2967-3010).

findings.claim: FFmpeg's segment muxer is a ready-made disk 'bucket' ring: segment_time defaults to 2 s, cuts are accurate only if keyframes are forced at those times, and segment_wrap reuses segment indices as a circular set of files.
findings.evidence: muxers.texi: 'segment_time ... Default value is "2" ... Note that splitting may not be accurate, unless you force the reference stream key-frames at the given time.' (L3630-3636); 'segment_wrap limit: Wrap around segment index once it reaches limit.' (L3708-3709); break_non_keyframes defaults to 0 (L3727).

findings.claim: Windows.Graphics.Capture frames carry a QPC timestamp, so the video can be timed in the same QPC domain as WASAPI audio and the clip window. No conversion through the adjustable wall clock is needed.
findings.evidence: Direct3D11CaptureFrame.SystemRelativeTime: 'The QPC (Query Performance Counter) time at which the compositor rendered the frame.'

findings.claim: A plain time-capped RAM ring of length N cannot produce N-before plus M-after by waiting M seconds and then saving: by then the first M seconds of the requested pre-roll have been evicted. Post-roll needs either (a) pinning or referencing the pre-roll at request time (OBS-style refcount copy, presumably what Overwolf capture(past, future) does internally), or (b) a buffer at least N+M+margins long (the Steam approach). The OBS delayed-save script workaround gets only buffer_length - M seconds of pre-roll unless the buffer is enlarged.
findings.evidence: Follows from OBS purge logic (eviction by max_time measured from the newest packet, L1031-1045) and from the forum workaround where the buffer must exceed the delay. Overwolf's internals are not public.

findings.claim: Storage sizing and SSD wear: encoded-packet buffers scale linearly with bitrate. At 40 Mbps (1440p60-class) RAM holds about 5 MB/s, so a 60 s ring is about 300 MB and one 44 s active clip adds about 220 MB. A continuous disk ring at 25-40 Mbps writes about 11-18 GB per hour of play. At 4 h/day that is roughly 16-26 TB/year, which fits typical consumer SSD endurance but is not negligible, and the temp files hold friends' Discord voice (a privacy issue).
findings.evidence: Arithmetic: Mbps / 8 = MB/s; 40/8 = 5 MB/s x 60 s = 300 MB; 25 Mbps = 3.125 MB/s x 3600 = 11.25 GB/h. Vendor TBW ratings were not retrieved (search budget exhausted).

findings.claim: Industry split on where the rolling buffer lives: RAM (OBS replay buffer, Overwolf replays) versus disk (NVIDIA temp-files buffer, AMD's default HDD buffer with an optional RAM mode, Steam's DASH segment folders). This supports offering RAM by default plus an optional disk 'bucket' mode.
findings.evidence: See the OBS deque-in-memory code, Overwolf turnOn 'captured in the memory', NVIDIA 'Temporary files location', AMD 'hard drive ... can be changed to system memory', and Steam .m4s/session.mpd folders (sources above). Medal's buffer storage was NOT found.

design_recommendations: CLOCK (matches the user's request): keep every packet timestamp in local QPC (WGC SystemRelativeTime and WASAPI QPC positions are already QPC). Define DuoClip global time as a mapping global = local_qpc + offset + skew*(local_qpc - t0), estimated NTP-style over the WebRTC data channel against one reference peer. Never use the Windows wall clock (GetSystemTime*, which NTP/w32time can step). Freeze the mapping and its error bound ε for each clip at request time and store both in the clip metadata, so a later re-estimate cannot shift an in-flight window.

CLIP REQUEST MESSAGE: {clip_id: UUIDv4, requester_id, seq, t_press_global_us, pre_s, post_s, margin_pre_s, margin_post_s, max_len_s, sync_error_us}. Send on a reliable, ordered data channel. Resend every 500 ms until ClipAck{clip_id, coverage}, persist outstanding requests across reconnects, and give up after 15 s. The receiver is idempotent on clip_id, so a duplicate only re-sends the ack.

WINDOW MATH (per PC): s_req = T - pre - margin_pre, e_req = T + post + margin_post (global). Local: s = toLocal(s_req) - ε, e = toLocal(e_req) + ε. Snap s down to the last IDR at or before s. Keep e as a timestamp; stream-copy can end on any frame when there are no B-frames. Otherwise end at the last frame whose references are all earlier, or at the next GOP boundary.

TWO-PHASE 'PIN THEN COLLECT' STATE MACHINE (both PCs): REQUESTED -> PINNED (immediately take refcounted references to all buffered packets of all tracks from keyframe(s) onward, like OBS's obs_encoder_packet_ref copy) -> COLLECTING (append live packets) -> FINALIZING -> READY. COLLECTING ends when every track (video plus each audio track) has emitted a packet with timestamp >= e, i.e. after encoder drain (OBS's sys_dts_usec >= save_ts rule generalized to all tracks, as in OBS mp4-mux's 'all tracks caught up' check). It also ends on a timeout of e + 3 s of QPC time, or when the source ends.

CRASH SAFETY / LOCAL 'BUCKET': as soon as a clip is PINNED, stream it on a low-priority I/O thread into %LOCALAPPDATA%\DuoClip\buckets\<clip_id>\full.mp4 as fragmented MP4. Use one fragment per GOP (FFmpeg movflags frag_keyframe+empty_moov+default_base_moof, or an OBS-Hybrid-MP4-style muxer), plus a small JSON journal (window, offsets, coverage, state). After a crash or game exit during post-roll the file is still decodable up to the last fragment, and the app recovers it on restart. Rewrite it as a regular MP4 (moov) on finalize.

DEFAULTS: pre 30 s (user range 10-120 s); post 10 s (presets 0/5/10/15/30 s); hidden margins +2 s pre and +2 s post, shown in the editor as slack beyond the default in/out handles; keyframe interval 1 s with closed GOP; B-frames 0, for minimal encoder delay and trivial end cuts (allow <=2 only if quality testing demands it); RAM ring 60 s or max(60 s, pre + margin_pre + GOP + 25 s request-delay tolerance), plus a size cap (e.g. 600 MB) that shortens the ring while warning the user; finalize timeout e + 3 s; maximum clip length including extensions 180 s (Overwolf treats over 3 min as not 'short'); at most 4 concurrent active clips.

PINNING MEMORY: pinned packets are excluded from ring eviction by refcount. They do not count against the ring's time limit but do count against a global memory budget (e.g. 1 GB). Once a pinned fragment is safely in the bucket file, drop the RAM reference, so long post-rolls stream to disk instead of growing RAM.

EXTEND/MERGE RULE: if the SAME requester presses again while their clip is PINNED or COLLECTING and the new window overlaps or is within 5 s of [s,e], extend: e = max(e, new_e), keep the clip_id, cap at max_len, and send ClipExtend{clip_id, seq+1, new_t_press} to the peer, which applies the same rule. A press by the OTHER friend creates its own clip_id, but both clips share the pinned packets and bucket fragments by refcount; the UI can offer 'merge'. This makes the merge decision deterministic on both PCs.

KEYFRAMES: do not force IDRs for normal operation; a fixed 1 s GOP plus outward snapping costs at most 1 s of slack, and the 2 s margins absorb it. For frame-accurate export, either re-encode the short clip, or stream-copy and hide the leading frames with an MP4 edit list, or smart-render only the first partial GOP. Optional use of forced IDR: on the press (or remote request arrival), force an IDR at the next frame (NVENC NV_ENC_PIC_FLAG_FORCEIDR with enablePTD=1 / AMF ForcePictureType=IDR / VPL MFX_FRAMETYPE_IDR / MF CODECAPI_AVEncVideoForceKeyFrame). Post-roll fragments then start on a clean boundary and segment files align across both PCs. Cost is one larger frame.

AUDIO/VIDEO INTERLEAVE: keep game and Discord as separate audio tracks timestamped in QPC. Collect audio until the last audio packet ends after e; AAC frames are about 21.3 ms at 48 kHz and Opus usually 20 ms (inferred, not verified here). Fill device or process gaps with silence packets so tracks never drift. Trim audio sample-accurately at export.

RAM vs DISK MODES: default 'RAM ring + per-clip disk bucket' gives the lowest SSD wear and privacy exposure, and crash safety once a clip exists. Optional 'Long history (Steam-like)' mode: a disk ring of 10 s fMP4 segment files (1 s fragments inside) in a dedicated folder, sized by GB (e.g. 10-30 min). Pin by refcount, or by hard-linking or renaming segment files into the clip bucket (O(1) on the same NTFS volume). The deleter skips pinned files. Wipe the folder on clean exit and at startup. Offer at-rest encryption, because the temp files contain friends' Discord voice.

REMOTE PC TIMING: on receipt of a request the remote PINS immediately, provided its ring still contains s, so tolerated delay = ring_len - (pre + margin_pre + GOP) (about 27 s with the defaults). It finalizes when its packets reach toLocal(T + post + margin_post) + ε, the same rule as the requester. If the request arrives after e already passed, finalize immediately from the ring/pins. Ack twice: once with 'pinned + expected coverage', then with 'ready + final coverage + byte size + proxy available'.

PARTIAL COVERAGE: never fail a clip because the start or end is missing. Return coverage intervals (e.g. [s_actual, e_actual] plus gaps[]). The editor draws 'no footage from <friend>' regions, and the clipper's default in/out stays on the global timeline.

TRANSFER: transfer the 720p proxy first, then fetch the trimmed full-quality range by fragment index (GOP-aligned byte ranges), so a dropped connection resumes from the last fragment and requests stay idempotent per (clip_id, fragment_idx). If the user's 'bucket' means cloud object storage, it can be a fallback relay for these same fragment objects with short auto-expiry; this is design inference only, as provider lifecycle docs were not verified here.
EDGE: same user presses again during post-roll -> extend the window with the same clip_id (cap 180 s) and send ClipExtend to the peer.
EDGE: both friends press within seconds -> two clip_ids sharing pinned data by refcount, with an optional 'merge' in the UI; no duplicated RAM.
EDGE: request reaches the remote late (network delay or retransmit) -> pin on arrival if the ring still covers s; finalize at e, or immediately if e already passed.
EDGE: request arrives after the remote ring evicted s, or the remote app or buffer started after s -> partial clip with coverage metadata; the editor shows the gap.

EDGE: data channel disconnects before the ack -> requester persists the request and re-sends on reconnect; the remote dedupes by clip_id. Apply the timeout only if the reconnect comes after the ring would have evicted s, and then mark the clip partial.

EDGE: game process exits or the WGC item is Closed during post-roll -> finalize early with the packets so far and mark the clip 'truncated_by_source_end'; the peer still finalizes its own side normally.
EDGE: DuoClip crashes during post-roll -> the bucket fMP4 plus journal survive; on restart, finalize as partial and notify the peer, whose request stays idempotent.
EDGE: window minimized or occluded, so WGC delivers no new frames -> video packets stop; use the e + 3 s timeout, or duplicate the last frame to keep CFR; audio continues.
EDGE: GPU driver reset, encoder error or device lost -> close the current fragment, record a gap, restart the encoder with an IDR, and keep collecting until e.
EDGE: clock offset re-estimated or stepped mid-clip -> the clip uses the offset frozen at request time; later corrections only adjust editor alignment metadata.
EDGE: peer just connected and sync has not converged (large ε) -> widen margins automatically to max(2 s, 3ε) and flag 'low-confidence sync' in the editor.
EDGE: disk full or bucket write fails -> keep the clip RAM-only, raise the memory budget temporarily for that clip, and warn the user; never stall the capture pipeline.
EDGE: the user sets a very long post-roll (over 30 s) -> stream to the bucket and drop RAM references after each fragment is written; enforce the max clip length.

EDGE: hotkey pressed with no active capture (game not running) -> reject locally with a toast; send no request to the peer, or send one marked 'requester_no_source' so the peer can still save its POV.

checks.claim: OBS's native replay buffer saves only footage from before the hotkey. save() stores save_ts = os_gettime_ns()/1000, and the file is cut at the first encoded packet whose sys_dts_usec >= save_ts, so there is no post-roll and the save waits out encoder latency. os_gettime_ns() is QueryPerformanceCounter on Windows, and libobs deliberately stamps encoder packets with system (QPC) time to keep encoders in sync.
checks.note: Re-read at obs-studio master commit 39c2de975bb94058553fe8da85cb991c28b37202 (the commit both researchers cite; it is still master today). Line 930 of obs-ffmpeg-mux.c sets 'stream->save_ts = os_gettime_ns() / 1000LL;'. Line 1227: 'if (stream->save_ts && packet->sys_dts_usec >= stream->save_ts)', then replay_buffer_save(). Lines 391-396 of platform-windows.c: os_gettime_ns() calls QueryPerformanceCounter and scales it with util_mul_div64. Lines 1408-1411 of obs-encoder.c carry the comment 'we use system time here to ensure sync with other encoders' and then set sys_dts_usec = dts_usec. No duration or post-roll parameter exists: the only procs are 'void save()' and 'get_last_replay' (lines 948-949). Primary source.

checks.claim: The OBS RAM ring evicts whole GOPs from the front and always keeps at least 2 keyframes. It is limited by max_time_sec and max_size_mb. Plugin defaults are 15 s / 500 MB and frontend defaults are 20 s / 512 MB.
checks.note: Most of this is confirmed. purge() pops packets until the next video keyframe (obs-ffmpeg-mux.c L1015-1029). Plugin defaults are max_time_sec 15 and max_size_mb 500 (L1241-1245). OBSBasic.cpp sets RecRBTime 20 and RecRBSize 512 for both SimpleOutput and AdvOut (L642-643, L685-686). The packets live in an in-memory deque. Correction: 'always keeps at least 2 keyframes' is not strictly guaranteed. replay_buffer_purge() checks 'stream->keyframes <= 2' only once, before its purge loop ('while ((pkt->dts_usec - stream->cur_time) > stream->max_time) purge(stream);', L1031-1045). The count is not re-checked inside the loop, so a GOP longer than max_time can take it below 2. With the planned 1 s GOP this never matters, and the design conclusion (a RAM ring with GOP-wise eviction, as in OBS) stands.

checks.claim: OBS 'pins' the saved range by taking refcounted copies of the buffered packets (obs_encoder_packet_ref) and muxing them on a separate thread while the live ring keeps evicting. A second save pressed while muxing is not dropped: save_ts stays set and the save fires on the first packet after muxing ends.
checks.note: insert_packet() calls obs_encoder_packet_ref (L1054). replay_buffer_save() sets muxing=true and spawns mux_thread (around L1172). In replay_buffer_data(), 'if (os_atomic_load_bool(&stream->muxing)) return;' runs before 'stream->save_ts = 0;' (L1227-1236), so a pending save is deferred, not lost. This supports the researchers' 'pin then collect' design. Primary source.

checks.claim: Default W32Time on standalone PCs is loose: SpecialPollInterval is 604,800 s but is clamped since build 1703 by MaxPollInterval=15 (32,768 s, about 9.1 h). MinPollInterval is 10, MaxAllowedPhaseOffset is 1 s (step above 1 s), PhaseCorrectRate is 7, UpdateInterval is 360,000, and Max{Neg,Pos}PhaseCorrection is 54,000 s. Microsoft's support boundary requires a special configuration plus <5 ms latency, stratum ≤5 and ≤6 hops for 50 ms, and says 'For 1 ms accuracy, you can't depend on a remote time sources'.
checks.note: Every registry default matches Windows-Time-Service-Tools-and-Settings.md: L338 (MaxAllowedPhaseOffset standalone 1), L340 (MaxNegPhaseCorrection standalone 54,000 = 15 h), L341 (MaxPollInterval standalone 15), L344 (MinPollInterval standalone 10), L345 (PhaseCorrectRate standalone 7), L349 (UpdateInterval standalone 360,000), L350 (UtilizeSslTimeData 1, except 0 on Server 2025), and L377 (SpecialPollInterval standalone 604,800, 'Starting with build 1703 ... contained by the MinPollInterval and MaxPollInterval'). The default NtpServer is 'time.windows.com, 0x9'; 0x1 is SpecialInterval, so the clamp applies. The effective nominal interval is therefore ~9.1 h exactly, not 'at best ~9 h'. Caution: the GPO table in the same doc (L278-301) lists different values (MaxPollInterval 10, SpecialPollInterval 1024). Those are Group Policy template defaults, not standalone registry defaults; don't mix them up. Support boundary: L55 (≤100 ms cumulative one-way latency for 1 s), L61-71 (50 ms tier) and L77-87 (1 ms tier: <0.1 ms latency, ≤4 hops, CPU ≤80%). accurate-time.md L35 has the 1 ms quote. Primary sources.

checks.claim: QPC is monotonic, independent of system time and UTC, and counts through sleep; ±10 ppm means ±36 ms/h. Both capture paths are QPC-native: WGC Direct3D11CaptureFrame.SystemRelativeTime is QPC, and WASAPI GetBuffer pu64QPCPosition is QPC converted to 100-ns units. In Rust, Instant uses QPC and SystemTime::now() uses GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime.
checks.note: acquiring-high-resolution-time-stamps.md says QPC 'isn't synchronized to, any external time reference' (L13), is 'completely independent of the system time and UTC' (L189) and 'does not go backward' (L273). L380 says it includes sleep, hibernate and connected standby, and the ±10 ppm table gives 1 hour ±36 ms and 1 day ±0.86 s (L459-465). The WGC doc says SystemRelativeTime is 'The QPC (Query Performance Counter) time at which the compositor rendered the frame.' The GetBuffer doc (L84-86, L221-225) gives *pu64QPCPosition = 10,000,000·t/f in 100-ns units. rust-lang/rust library/std/src/sys/pal/windows/time.rs L29 calls QueryPerformanceCounter, and library/std/src/sys/time/windows.rs L77 calls GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime. New caveat that matters for the design: the GetBuffer QPC semantics are documented generically, and nothing documents how they behave under process loopback, so measure it. AUDIOCLIENT_PROCESS_LOOPBACK_PARAMS lists 'req.target-min-winverclnt: Windows 10 Build 20348', and the ApplicationLoopback sample README (L41) says it 'requires Windows 10 build 20348 or later'. OBS's win-wasapi gates process capture at build 19041 with the comment 'MS says 20348, but process filtering seems to work earlier' (plugins/win-wasapi/plugin-main.cpp L43-51).

contradictions_between_researchers: Where the global clock comes from. Researcher 1 makes UTC the canonical timescale, taken from an in-app NTS client (NTP.br and Cloudflare) disciplining QPC, with P2P pings only as a cross-check and refinement. Researcher 3 defines global time purely peer-to-peer: global = local_qpc + offset + skew·(…), estimated NTP-style over the WebRTC data channel against one reference peer, with no external UTC source. These are different architectures with different failure modes: Researcher 3's breaks when the reference peer leaves, and Researcher 1's breaks when UDP 123 or TCP 4460 is blocked. The plan must pick one or adopt Researcher 1's hybrid explicitly.

How corrections are applied. Researcher 1 recommends re-mapping every clip retroactively, with a two-sided regression over sync samples from before and after it, written back to the clip metadata. Researcher 3 says to freeze the mapping and its error at request time so a later re-estimate cannot shift an in-flight window; later corrections only adjust editor alignment metadata. They can be reconciled (frozen mapping for choosing the capture window, refined mapping for alignment), but as written they disagree.

Safety margins. Researcher 1 sets margin = relative clock uncertainty + one GOP (1 s), in milliseconds plus 1 s. Researcher 3 uses fixed hidden margins of 2 s per side, auto-widened to max(2 s, 3ε), plus a 60 s ring sized to tolerate ~27 s of request delay.

What 'bucket' means and which transport is primary. Researcher 2 reads it as cloud object storage and recommends bucket-first on R2, with WebRTC P2P only as an opportunistic accelerator ('a TURN relay is never needed'). Researcher 3 assumed a local per-clip disk folder, made P2P fragment transfer the main path, and mentions a cloud bucket only as an optional fallback relay ('design inference only').

Transfer unit. Researcher 2 uses separately encrypted 4-8 MiB chunk objects plus an encrypted manifest keyed to global-clock ranges. Researcher 3 uses GOP-aligned fMP4 fragment indices and byte ranges, idempotent per (clip_id, fragment_idx). The chunk boundaries and indexing schemes are incompatible unless unified.

Clip size feeding the cost model. Researcher 2's estimate assumes 60 MB per clip. Researcher 3's defaults (30 s pre + 10 s post + 2×2 s margins = 44 s, at 40 Mbps ≈ 5 MB/s) give about 220 MB per full-quality clip. At Researcher 3's numbers, egress-billed providers (S3, GCS, Supabase, B2) would cost about 3.7× Researcher 2's figures, unless only the 720p proxy plus the trimmed range is uploaded, as Researcher 2 also suggests. R2 stays cheap because egress is free, but storage and Class A estimates scale too.

Disk use by default. Researcher 2 makes the RAM ring the default, with disk 'time buckets' as an opt-in setting because of SSD wear. Researcher 3 also keeps the ring in RAM, but by default streams every pinned clip immediately to a crash-safe fMP4 in %LOCALAPPDATA%. The two disagree on whether clip data touches disk before the user exports.
verification.corrections_summary:
I re-checked 18 decision-relevant claims against primary sources: GitHub source and docs repos, the AWS Price List API, the GCS pricing page, the gcloud CLI help, crates.io and a crate tarball, and the IANA tz leap-seconds list. Nothing core was refuted. Most of the claims labeled 'primary' hold exactly, line references included.

Confirmed:
- OBS's replay buffer is past-only. It uses QPC timestamps, an in-RAM deque of encoded packets evicted GOP by GOP, refcount pinning, and a separate mux thread.
- Overwolf's capture(pastDuration, futureDuration) API exists and holds the buffer in memory.
- Steamworks Timeline describes clips covering time 'before and after' an event.
- W32Time standalone defaults: SpecialPollInterval 604,800 s clamped to 2^15 s ≈ 9.1 h, and a 1 s step threshold. Microsoft's support-boundary tiers are as quoted.
- QPC timestamps are native to WGC and WASAPI. Rust's Instant uses QPC and SystemTime uses GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime.

1. OBS does not strictly 'always keep 2 keyframes'. keyframes<=2 is an entry guard checked once before the purge loop. This is irrelevant with a 1 s GOP.

gaps.gap: No consent or privacy flow exists for remote-triggered capture. In the design, friend A's hotkey makes friend B's PC save and upload B's footage and audio, with no interaction from B. gaps.gap: Neither hybrid-GPU laptops nor the 'zero-copy' claim has been validated. On MUX-less Optimus or AMD hybrid laptops, which are common among Brazilian gamers, DWM composes on the iGPU, so WGC surfaces live on the display adapter while NVENC lives on the dGPU. That forces a cross-adapter copy or iGPU encoding. Even on desktops, a 2-buffer WGC pool has to be released quickly while hardware encoding runs asynchronously, and a BGRA-to-NV12 pass (or the encoder's internal ARGB conversion) is always required. So 'zero-copy' means at best one GPU pass, and that is unmeasured.
gaps.why_it_matters: These are the main FPS-impact claims behind 'WGC is most effective'. A silent CPU readback on a laptop would contradict the minimal-FPS-impact requirement.
gaps.suggested_resolution: Prototype and measure with PresentMon and GPUView on four setups: desktop NVIDIA, desktop AMD, a MUX-less Optimus laptop, and an Intel iGPU-only PC. Read how Sunshine handles adapter mismatch in src/platform/windows/display_wgc.cpp and display_vram.cpp (adapter selection and cross-adapter copy). Set a policy: encode on the adapter that owns the WGC surface (QSV/AMF on the iGPU), or do an explicit GPU-to-GPU copy, chosen per measured cost.

gaps.why_it_matters: Continuous CPU encoding while gaming contradicts the 'minimal FPS impact' requirement. These users would get a poor experience or no product.
gaps.suggested_resolution: Check AMD's and NVIDIA's spec pages and the Steam Hardware Survey (Portuguese-Brazil filter) for how common these cards are. Decide on a fallback: an iGPU encoder via cross-adapter copy if one exists, otherwise a reduced 720p30 x264 'superfast' mode with a clear warning, or an explicit 'not supported' message.

gaps.gap: Brazilian legal obligations beyond LGPD were not researched. From prior knowledge, needing verification because the search budget was exhausted: Marco Civil da Internet (Lei 12.965/2014) Art. 15 requires application providers acting with an economic purpose to keep access logs for 6 months. The ECA Digital (Lei 15.211/2025, reportedly in force since ~March 2026) imposes age assurance, parental tools and privacy-by-default on digital services likely to be used by minors, and gamers include many minors. LGPD Art. 14 requires parental consent for children's data.

gaps.gap: Ring and clip behaviour across capture-size changes is unspecified. When the game changes resolution or toggles windowed/fullscreen, WGC ContentSize changes, so the frame pool is recreated, the encoder may restart with new SPS/PPS, and the two POVs end up at different sizes. A clip spanning the change would contain multiple parameter sets or sample descriptions, which many players and editors handle badly.

If a re-init is unavoidable, cut the ring segment there, and on export either re-encode or split at the boundary. Add this to the edge-case list and test it.

critic.overall_assessment:
OBS is answered definitively for request (4). The evidence is primary: OBS source at commit c5bcbca. Game Capture is DLL injection. Window Capture's automatic mode prefers BitBlt and uses WGC only for listed window classes. Display Capture prefers DXGI and switches to WGC for hybrid or cross-GPU setups. Game Capture has no WGC fallback.

Medal is only answered at secondary confidence. Third-party 2023 logs show an injected, OBS-derived hook as the default, with WGC as the opt-in 'Advanced Window Capture'. I added one new piece of static evidence from the third-party medal-cross-platform repo. The 2026 recorder still carries the OBS hook IPC classes, and scope.dll has an external-texture capture target. MedalEncoder.exe itself imports no injection APIs, so any injection would run through the Host helpers. It also implements hotkeys with SetWindowsHookEx. None of this shows what the 2026 build does by default at runtime, and Medal's marketing contradicts it. A black-box runtime test on a team member's own PC (hook DLL presence plus log state names), or a direct statement from Medal, would settle it.

The gaps that would most change the design are:
- An explicit minimum-OS decision. Windows 10 may lack borderless WGC, process loopback is shaky there, and Windows 10 ESU is ending, which could flip the Windows 10 default from WGC to DDA-crop.
- A consent model for remote-triggered capture.
- The missing own-microphone track and the Discord-voice duplication and offset problem.
- An anti-cheat test plan that includes the Brazilian vendors Gamers Club and FACEIT, and every non-capture touchpoint with the game.
- Hotkey implementation and elevated games.
- Validating 'zero-copy' on hybrid-GPU laptops, plus GPUs with no hardware encoder.
- HDR.
- The unresolved time-architecture choice, which needs a numeric accuracy target.
- Confirming with the user what 'bucket' means.
